devils-hole-pupfish.funFact: It has no pelvic fins, the males shine a metallic blue, and the entire wild population feeds and breeds on one small, shallow rock shelf.
devils-hole-pupfish.revealFact: It lives only in Devils Hole, a water-filled limestone cavern in Nevada's Ash Meadows, where irrigation in the 1960s and 1970s lowered the water and exposed its spawning shelf. The fight over that groundwater went all the way to the US Supreme Court.

hints.habitat: The upper waters of one deep, water-filled limestone cavern, around a shallow rock ledge
hints.size: Up to about 3.4 cm long
hints.diet: Nearly everything on offer: beetles, snails, algae and small freshwater crustaceans

alabama-cavefish.funFact: Females carry their eggs inside their gill chambers, and its fragile food web runs on the droppings of a colony of bats roosting overhead.
alabama-cavefish.revealFact: Found only in Key Cave in north-western Alabama, it may be the rarest freshwater fish of all: fewer than 100 are thought to remain, and surveys of 120 other caves nearby have never turned up another.

hints.habitat: Underground pools of groundwater in a single cave system
hints.size: Up to about 7.2 cm long

giant-sea-bass.funFact: Juveniles start out bright red or orange before fading to gray or brown, and despite their bulk, adults can dart fast enough to outpace a bonito.
giant-sea-bass.revealFact: It ranges from Humboldt Bay, California, south to the Gulf of California, and is most common from Point Conception southward. Heavy fishing nearly wiped it out off Southern California by the 1980s before it was given protection.

hints.habitat: Rocky bottoms, kelp forests and drop-offs near the shore
hints.size: Up to about 250 cm (2.5 m) long
hints.diet: Crustaceans such as crabs, plus many fish including anchovies, croakers and mackerel

cui-ui.funFact: This big sucker can live for around 40 years but doesn't start breeding until it is at least eight, and it dines mostly on tiny zooplankton.
cui-ui.revealFact: It lives only in Pyramid Lake, Nevada, and must run up the lower Truckee River to spawn, because eggs laid in the salty lake rarely succeed. Its other home, Winnemucca Lake, dried up in the 20th century.

hints.habitat: Deep water of a large, somewhat salty lake; spawns by migrating up an inflowing river
hints.size: Up to about 67 cm long
hints.diet: Mainly zooplankton, and possibly tiny algae and diatoms

razorback-sucker.funFact: It is named for the sharp-edged keel that rises behind its head, and a complete fossil skeleton from the Early Pliocene still shows off that same hump.
razorback-sucker.revealFact: Once found throughout the Colorado River basin and down into Mexico, it now survives mainly in the Colorado above the Grand Canyon and in reservoirs such as Lakes Mead, Mohave and Havasu. Dams, habitat loss and commercial fishing drove its decline.

hints.habitat: Backwaters and deep pools near strong current in medium to large rivers, plus reservoirs
hints.size: Up to about 91 cm long

humpback-chub.funFact: The bump behind its head is thought to steer water over its body so it can hold its place in swift currents, and its skin is almost entirely scaleless.
humpback-chub.revealFact: It survives in just six population centres in the Colorado River system, including the Grand Canyon and the Little Colorado River in Arizona and canyons in Utah and Colorado. Habitat loss, such as from Glen Canyon Dam, cut its numbers dramatically.

hints.habitat: Swift, rocky runs and turbulent pools in steep, high-gradient stretches of large rivers
hints.size: Up to about 38 cm long
hints.diet: Mostly invertebrates, plus some smaller fish

alabama-sturgeon.funFact: Biologists knew of this yellowish-orange sturgeon for decades, but it was mistaken for the shovelnose sturgeon until it was formally named as its own species in 1991.
alabama-sturgeon.revealFact: It once lived across the Mobile River basin, including the Alabama, Tombigbee, Cahaba and Coosa rivers, but is now believed to survive only in a short stretch of the lower Alabama River.

hints.habitat: The sandy, gravelly bottom of a large flowing river
hints.diet: Aquatic insects such as mayflies, caddisflies and dragonflies, plus small fish (about a third of its diet)

american-paddlefish.funFact: Its paddle-shaped snout stretches nearly a third of its body length and is covered with tens of thousands of sensory receptors for finding swarms of zooplankton.
american-paddlefish.revealFact: Native to the Mississippi River basin and neighbouring Gulf Coast drainages, it is the last living paddlefish, since its only modern relative, from China's Yangtze, is considered extinct. Overfishing, habitat destruction, pollution and poaching have shrunk its range.

hints.habitat: Slow-flowing big rivers, backwaters, oxbow lakes and reservoirs
hints.size: Up to about 221 cm (2.2 m) long
hints.diet: Plankton, mainly zooplankton, filtered from the water

diamond-darter.funFact: It is named for the sparkle it reflects when scientists collect it at night, and its see-through body is patterned in olive.
diamond-darter.revealFact: Once recorded from several Ohio River tributaries, including the Cumberland, Green and Muskingum, it is now known only from the Elk River in West Virginia. It was listed as endangered in 2013.

hints.habitat: The tail ends of riffles and heads of pools, with moderate flow over sand, gravel and cobble
hints.size: Up to about 7.7 cm long (standard length)

california-golden-trout.funFact: Its golden flanks are striped with red bands and about ten dark oval 'parr marks' on each side, and its fins have white leading edges.
california-golden-trout.revealFact: It is native to the southern Sierra Nevada of California, in Golden Trout Creek, Volcano Creek and the South Fork Kern River. It has been California's official state freshwater fish since 1947.

hints.habitat: Clear, cool mountain headwaters, creeks and lakes above about 2,100 m elevation
hints.size: Up to about 71 cm long

apache-trout.funFact: Two small black dots on either side of each pupil give it the look of wearing a dark mask across its eyes.
apache-trout.revealFact: Arizona's state fish is native to headwater streams of the White, Black and Little Colorado rivers in the White Mountains. It was among the first species protected under US endangered species law, and its numbers are still rising.

hints.habitat: Clear, cool mountain streams through conifer forest, generally above 2,500 m elevation
hints.size: Up to about 58 cm long
hints.diet: Land and aquatic insects such as caddisflies and true flies; in lakes also small fish and zooplankton

spring-pygmy-sunfish.funFact: It was written off as extinct after its first known spring was flooded by a reservoir in 1938, then turned up alive 35 years later. Breeding males are dark with shimmering blue-green bars.
spring-pygmy-sunfish.revealFact: It lives only in spring-fed wetlands of northern Alabama, chiefly the Beaverdam Spring complex in Limestone County, with a second population found in 2015 at Wheeler National Wildlife Refuge.

hints.habitat: Clear spring heads, spring pools and their weedy, spring-fed wetlands
hints.size: Rarely more than about an inch (2.5 cm) long
hints.diet: Probably tiny aquatic invertebrates such as amphipods, isopods and insect larvae

delta-smelt.funFact: This see-through little fish lives only about a year, which makes it so sensitive to change that it serves as a gauge of its whole ecosystem's health.
delta-smelt.revealFact: It is endemic to the upper Sacramento–San Joaquin estuary of California, where large-scale water pumping and habitat loss have left it functionally extinct in the wild.

hints.habitat: Open, low-salinity channels of an estuary where fresh and salt water mix
hints.size: Up to about 12 cm long
hints.diet: Zooplankton

moapa-dace.funFact: Its tiny scales are sunk into its skin, giving it a leathery feel, and that is exactly what its scientific name means in Latin.
moapa-dace.revealFact: It lives only in the warm springs and upper reaches of the Muddy (formerly Moapa) River in southern Nevada. The Moapa National Wildlife Refuge was set up just for it, the first US refuge created to protect an endangered fish.

hints.habitat: Shaded pools of warm, spring-fed headwater streams over gravel, sand and mud
hints.size: Up to about 9 cm long
hints.diet: Omnivorous

copper-redhorse.funFact: Unlike its relatives, it has molar-like throat teeth for crushing hard-shelled bivalves, and it shows off a bright red tail fin.
copper-redhorse.revealFact: It is found only in south-western Quebec, in the St Lawrence and Richelieu rivers and the Rivière des Mille Îles, and its tiny range has shrunk sharply in recent decades.

hints.habitat: Rocky pools, backwaters and runs of medium-sized rivers that warm above 20 °C in summer
hints.size: Up to about 72 cm long
hints.depth: Spawns in riffles about 0.75–2 m deep
hints.diet: Hard-shelled bivalves

atlantic-whitefish.funFact: Its lineage split from all other whitefish about 15 million years ago, and nobody has ever seen it reproduce in the wild.
atlantic-whitefish.revealFact: It survives only as landlocked populations in lakes of the Petite Rivière watershed in Nova Scotia; sea-run fish in the Tusket and Annis rivers are gone. Dams and introduced predators such as smallmouth bass and chain pickerel made it critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Open water of freshwater lakes; historically also migrated between rivers and coastal estuaries
hints.size: Up to about 40 cm long
hints.diet: Insects and small fish

widemouth-blindcat.funFact: It is the only species in a genus named Satan, and although it has eye remnants, its optic tract fades out before ever reaching the brain.
widemouth-blindcat.revealFact: It is known only from five artesian wells that tap the San Antonio Pool of the Edwards Aquifer in Texas, where groundwater pollution threatens it.

hints.habitat: Deep, lightless underground water, reached only through artesian wells
hints.size: Up to about 13.7 cm long
hints.diet: Probably crustaceans (their shells have been found in its stomach)

comanche-springs-pupfish.funFact: Males wear a striking speckled pattern instead of the vertical bars their relatives sport, and the species was described way back in 1853.
comanche-springs-pupfish.revealFact: Named for Comanche Springs in Fort Stockton, Texas, which went dry in 1955, it now survives only in spring systems near Balmorhea, such as San Solomon and Giffin springs. Part of its habitat is a spring whose head was turned into a concrete-lined swimming pool.

hints.habitat: Springs, spring-fed marshes and irrigation canals, usually over mud in flowing water
hints.size: Up to about 6.2 cm long

vancouver-lamprey.funFact: Adults latch onto young trout and salmon to feed on their body fluids, yet only about 15% of their hosts are fatally wounded.
vancouver-lamprey.revealFact: It lives only in Cowichan Lake and neighbouring Mesachie Lake on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, with perhaps 1,000 to 2,000 adults in all. Unlike the Pacific lamprey it descends from, it never migrates and stays in fresh water.

hints.habitat: Shallow gravel shores of freshwater lakes; larvae live in silt and sand in still water
hints.size: Up to about 27.3 cm long
hints.diet: Body fluids of other fish, especially young cutthroat trout and coho salmon

tequila-splitfin.funFact: Females give birth to live young, up to 29 per brood, and adult males flash a crescent-shaped red-orange or yellow band on the tail.
tequila-splitfin.revealFact: It is endemic to the Ameca River basin in Jalisco, Mexico, and by the early 2000s survived only in one tiny spring pool at Teuchitlán. After years of reintroduction work it now thrives at home again, and its name comes from the nearby Tequila Volcano.

hints.habitat: Quiet, shallow water over mud and silt in a spring-fed river and pool
hints.size: Up to about 6 cm long

butterfly-splitfin.funFact: Males' fins flush with stronger color when they get excited, and newborns spend their first couple of weeks entirely silvery.
butterfly-splitfin.revealFact: It comes from the upper Río Ameca basin around Teuchitlán in Jalisco, Mexico, historically an area only about 15 km across. Once an aquarium favourite, it is now rated critically endangered by the IUCN.

hints.habitat: Springs and small streams of hard, alkaline water over limestone bedrock
hints.size: Up to about 8 cm long

rainbow-characodon.funFact: Mothers nourish their developing young through a placenta-like structure, then give birth to 5–20 free-swimming fry after about 55 days.
rainbow-characodon.revealFact: It is native to just a few springs and streams of the upper Río Tunal around Durango, Mexico, such as the Abraham González spring and the El Salto waterfall area. Invasive species keep threatening its tiny range.

hints.habitat: Clear, shallow springs and marshes with little current and plenty of submerged plants
hints.size: Up to about 4 cm long
hints.diet: Algae

totoaba.funFact: It is the biggest member of the drum family and the only living species in its genus. Youngsters are spotted, while adults turn silvery with darker fins.
totoaba.revealFact: Endemic to Mexico's Gulf of California, it spawns and raises its young in the upper Gulf near the Colorado River delta, a habitat changed by damming of the river. Nearly 50 years of overfishing drove its decline.

hints.habitat: Soft, sandy coastal sea floor; young in river mouths and near rocky shores
hints.size: Up to about 200 cm (2 m) long
hints.diet: Fish and shrimp

cuban-gar.funFact: It shrugs off high ammonia levels, can breathe some air when the water runs low on oxygen, and adults hunt fish and even birds.
cuban-gar.revealFact: It lives in rivers, lakes and swamps of western Cuba, including the Zapata Swamp, and on the Isla de la Juventud. Overfishing, habitat loss and introduced largemouth bass, which prey on its young, have made it critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Slow rivers, lakes and floodplains; it also tolerates brackish water
hints.size: Up to about 200 cm (2 m) long
hints.diet: Other fish and even birds

monterrey-platyfish.funFact: This drab little livebearer looks a lot like a female guppy, and it has proven trickier to keep in captivity than most of its relatives.
monterrey-platyfish.revealFact: It was native to a tiny part of the Río San Juan system around Monterrey, Mexico, until urban sprawl, drying springs and pollution wiped out its wild habitat. Now extinct in the wild, it survives in captive 'safety populations' kept by universities, public aquariums and hobbyists.

hints.habitat: Springs and small headwater streams
hints.size: Up to about 4 cm long

minckleys-cichlid.funFact: Its colors can shift within seconds during fights or courtship, and some individuals are deep-bodied while others are slender.
minckleys-cichlid.revealFact: It is endemic to the spring pools of the butterfly-shaped Cuatro Ciénegas basin in Coahuila, Mexico, a place with very high levels of endemism. It honours ichthyologist Wendell Minckley, who studied the basin's ecology.

hints.habitat: Clear spring-fed pools with plant and rock cover in a very dry basin
hints.size: Up to about 17.5 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Snails and small fish

clarion-angelfish.funFact: Juveniles are yellowish-orange with blue bars that fade away as they grow into orange-and-brown adults with a vermilion tail.
clarion-angelfish.revealFact: It is largely restricted to the Revillagigedo Islands off western Mexico, with occasional strays at the tip of Baja California and at Clipperton Island. Collecting it became illegal once the islands were protected, but captive-bred fish now supply the aquarium trade.

hints.habitat: Rocky reefs, alone or in shoals
hints.size: Up to about 20 cm long

splendid-toadfish.funFact: Unlike any other toadfish, it is vividly colored with bright yellow-edged fins, and it makes a buzzing mating call that divers can hear.
splendid-toadfish.revealFact: Once thought to live only around Cozumel Island, Mexico, it has since been found on reefs from Honduras north to Cancún.

hints.habitat: Dens under coral outcrops and in rocky reef caves, often marked by a sloping sand patch
hints.size: Up to about 24 cm long
hints.diet: Small fish, snails and polychaete worms

gulf-grouper.funFact: Adults can quickly change color to mimic their blotchy juvenile pattern, and they have been reported to prey on young hammerhead sharks.
gulf-grouper.revealFact: It is endemic to Mexican waters from Baja California Sur south to Mazatlán, including the whole Gulf of California and the Revillagigedo Islands. Commercial fishing has cut its numbers sharply since the mid-20th century.

hints.habitat: Rocky reefs, kelp beds and seamounts
hints.size: Up to about 198 cm (2 m) long
hints.diet: Fish, lobsters and slipper lobsters, even young hammerhead sharks

nassau-grouper.funFact: Known as the least wary and friendliest of all groupers, it 'inhales' prey with its big mouth, and up to 30,000 may gather at one site to spawn.
nassau-grouper.revealFact: It lives on reefs of the western Atlantic, from Bermuda, Florida and the Bahamas through the Caribbean to Venezuela. Because it returns to the same spawning sites every year, fishing those gatherings has made it critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Coral reefs, often close to caves; juveniles in seagrass beds
hints.size: Up to about 122 cm (1.2 m) long
hints.diet: Mostly fish and crabs, plus other crustaceans and molluscs

arrow-cichlid.funFact: Unlike its yellow-tinted relatives it is silver to greenish gray, and breeding adults can turn completely black.
arrow-cichlid.revealFact: It lives only in Lake Apoyo, a volcanic crater lake in Nicaragua, where genetic evidence suggests it and five close relatives evolved side by side within the same lake.

hints.habitat: A single volcanic crater lake
hints.size: Up to about 20 cm long

sulphur-molly.funFact: Its water is so laced with toxic hydrogen sulfide that it spends most of its time breathing at the surface, and it makes waves to avoid hunting birds.
sulphur-molly.revealFact: It is endemic to the sulfur springs of Baños del Azufre near Teapa, on the border of the Mexican states of Tabasco and Chiapas. It is one of the few fish able to withstand such toxic water.

hints.habitat: Toxic sulfur springs and their outflow stream
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm long

blind-swamp-eel.funFact: Its describer loved giving cave fish devilish names, so he first called it Pluto infernalis, from the Latin for Hell. It has no eyes, no scales and no pigment.
blind-swamp-eel.revealFact: It is endemic to water-filled sinkholes and limestone caves of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, turning up in only about 7% of caves searched. Sewage and wastewater seeping into the aquifer threaten it.

hints.habitat: Shallow, muddy water in sinkholes and limestone caves, often under stones
hints.diet: Bat and swallow droppings, plus shrimp

bartons-cichlid.funFact: In breeding season males darken to a deep black, making them look like they are wearing a tuxedo, and the species was briefly placed in a genus named Nosferatu.
bartons-cichlid.revealFact: It is endemic to freshwater springs of the upper Panuco basin in San Luis Potosí, Mexico, especially the La Media Luna spring lagoon and the upper Río Verde.

hints.habitat: Clear springs, spring lagoons and rivers with plant and rock cover
hints.size: Up to about 18 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Smaller fish, aquatic insects, algae and other invertebrates

zebra-pleco.funFact: It goes by two aquarium code numbers, L-046 and L-098, and fathers guard the eggs until the fry swim off about a week later.
zebra-pleco.revealFact: It lives only along a small stretch of the Rio Xingu's big bend below Altamira, Brazil, where the Belo Monte Dam has severely reduced the river's flow. Exporting it from Brazil has been illegal since 2004.

hints.habitat: Fast-flowing, oxygen-rich rocky rapids full of caves and crevices
hints.size: Up to about 7 cm long
hints.diet: Small invertebrates such as insect larvae

naked-characin.funFact: Young fish have tiny, delicate scales that get reabsorbed into the skin, so adults end up scaleless with a greasy, spongy-looking hide.
naked-characin.revealFact: It lives only in the warm, spring-fed headwaters of the Valcheta Stream in northern Patagonia, Argentina, making it the southernmost characin. Invasive Uruguay tetras and rainbow trout threaten its tiny range.

hints.habitat: Headwaters of a small stream fed by a thermal spring
hints.size: Up to about 7.5 cm long

white-blotched-river-stingray.funFact: The venom in its tail spine gets weaker as it ages, while its jaws grow stiffer so older rays can crunch hard-shelled prey.
white-blotched-river-stingray.revealFact: It is endemic to the Xingu River basin in Brazil, where it prefers clear water over rocky bottoms.

hints.habitat: Clear rivers with rocky bottoms; buries itself in sand by day
hints.size: Up to about 111 cm across the disc
hints.diet: Bottom-dwelling invertebrates, hunted at night

ascotan-pupfish.funFact: Its entire species is spread across just 12 springs, and unlike some of its killifish kin, it is not a seasonal killifish.
ascotan-pupfish.revealFact: It is endemic to 12 springs fringing the Salar de Ascotán, a salt flat in the high Andes of Chile's Antofagasta Region.

hints.habitat: Small springs at the edge of a salt flat
hints.size: Up to about 7.5 cm long

brazilian-blind-characid.funFact: When undisturbed it hovers almost motionless in midwater with its body tilted at 10–40°, and in aquariums individuals ignore each other completely.
brazilian-blind-characid.revealFact: It is known only from groundwater in the karst near Jaíba, northern Minas Gerais, Brazil, where water extraction has dried many wells and springs. After a single specimen in 1962, it was not found again until 2004.

hints.habitat: Underground water in limestone karst, reached through caves and shallow wells
hints.size: Up to about 2.4 cm long (standard length)

brazilian-guitarfish.funFact: Its eggs lie dormant inside the mother for months before developing, and it is the only known host of a parasitic flatworm nicknamed 'Good Luck'.
brazilian-guitarfish.revealFact: It lives on the continental shelf of southern Brazil, ranging south to northern Argentina, and was traditionally the main ray caught there. Trawling and netting, which take mostly pregnant females, have cut its numbers by more than 80% since 1986.

hints.habitat: Coastal waters across the continental shelf, from the shoreline to the shelf edge
hints.size: Up to about 138 cm (1.4 m) long
hints.diet: Crustaceans, cephalopods, polychaete worms and small fish

angular-angelshark.funFact: This shark is shaped like a ray, and adult males carry patches of small spines on their pectoral fins that are thought to help them hold females while mating.
angular-angelshark.revealFact: It lives along the coasts of Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina in the south-western Atlantic, where overfishing has made this bottom-dweller endangered.

hints.habitat: Sandy or muddy sea floor in coastal and shelf waters, sometimes brackish
hints.size: Up to about 129 cm (1.3 m) long
hints.diet: Mainly bony fish, plus crustaceans and molluscs

doce-surubim.funFact: This catfish is the largest native fish of its home river system, and it hangs out in the deepest parts of the main channels.
doce-surubim.revealFact: It is native to the Rio Doce basin in Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo, Brazil, where it was once common throughout the basin but is now endangered.

hints.habitat: The deepest parts of river channels and their main tributaries
hints.size: Up to about 42 cm long (standard length)

flame-tetra.funFact: It was already being sold as an aquarium fish in 1920, four years before scientists formally described it. Its back half glows flame red.
flame-tetra.revealFact: Native to coastal streams of Rio de Janeiro and the upper Tietê basin of São Paulo in south-eastern Brazil, it has declined badly from habitat loss, pollution and introduced fish such as tilapia. Huge numbers are now bred in captivity for aquariums.

hints.habitat: Small, slow, shallow and weedy streams shaded by forest
hints.size: Up to about 2.6 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Small insects, worms and plants

pacama.funFact: Its enormous mouth earned it the nickname 'Pac-Man catfish', and fathers look after the sticky eggs.
pacama.revealFact: It comes from the São Francisco River basin in Brazil, and Brazil's Ministry of the Environment considers it threatened.

hints.habitat: Still or slow-moving river waters, where it sits quietly on the bottom
hints.size: Up to about 72 cm long
hints.diet: Smaller fish

jumandi-cave-catfish.funFact: Its skin is studded with tiny denticles that can sense water flow, handy in a home that never sees daylight. Its eyes are minute and it has no pigment.
jumandi-cave-catfish.revealFact: It is endemic to the Jumandí Cave in the Napo River basin of Ecuador, living in the pitch-dark zone 300 m to 2 km in from the entrance.

hints.habitat: Permanently dark cave streams, hiding in holes among rocks
hints.size: Up to about 7 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Mayfly nymphs

danube-salmon.funFact: This big predator eats mostly fish, but adults also go after amphibians, reptiles, small mammals and waterfowl.
danube-salmon.revealFact: The huchen is endemic to the Danube basin, with most remaining fish in upper tributaries such as the Inn, Drava and Mur, plus rivers like the Sava and Drina. Dams that cut fish off from their spawning grounds are its main threat.

hints.habitat: Deeper stretches of swift, cold, oxygen-rich rivers
hints.size: Up to about 150 cm (1.5 m) long
hints.diet: Mostly fish, plus amphibians, reptiles, small mammals and waterfowl; young eat invertebrates

corfu-toothcarp.funFact: This short-lived little fish prefers fresh water, yet in lab tests it has coped with salinity as high as 46 parts per thousand.
corfu-toothcarp.revealFact: Despite its name, it has vanished from Corfu and Lefkas and now survives in springs and coastal wetlands of western Greece and southern Albania. Introduced species and water abstraction threaten it.

hints.habitat: Springs, swamps, lagoons and slow, weedy lowland streams
hints.size: Up to about 8 cm long
hints.diet: Mainly insects, especially chironomid midges

valencia-toothcarp.funFact: This sociable little carnivore forms small shoals, and males show off orange-rimmed fins.
valencia-toothcarp.revealFact: It is endemic to marshes, springs and irrigation channels of the Valencian Community and southern Catalonia, Spain. An aquarium in Valencia now breeds it for release into the nearby l'Albufera lagoon.

hints.habitat: Marshes, springs, lagoons and irrigation ditches with little current and plenty of vegetation
hints.size: Up to about 8 cm long
hints.diet: Crustaceans, insects and their larvae, and worms

adriatic-sturgeon.funFact: Its four barbels sit closer to the tip of its snout than to its mouth, and its body is armoured with five rows of bony scutes.
adriatic-sturgeon.revealFact: It is native to the Adriatic Sea and its large rivers, chiefly the Po and Adige in Italy, and once ranged down the eastern coast to Albania and Greece. Habitat destruction, pollution and overfishing have made it critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Large, deep rivers, estuaries and the near-shore sea over sand and mud
hints.size: Up to about 200 cm (2 m) long
hints.diet: Bottom-living invertebrates and small fish

european-sea-sturgeon.funFact: It can live to 100 years, and the last known wild hatching, in 1994, came from just a single mating pair.
european-sea-sturgeon.revealFact: Once found along coasts all over Europe, it now breeds only in the Garonne–Dordogne (Gironde) system of south-western France, with fewer than 800 mature wild fish estimated. Reintroductions are under way in the Rhine and Elbe.

hints.habitat: Coastal seas and estuaries, entering large rivers to spawn
hints.size: Up to about 600 cm (6 m) long
hints.diet: Polychaete worms and crustaceans, found with its sensitive barbels

ohrid-trout.funFact: Its lake may hold up to four forms of this trout, each breeding in its own place and season, though genetic data have not confirmed the split.
ohrid-trout.revealFact: It is endemic to Lake Ohrid on the border of North Macedonia and Albania, along with its inflows and the Black Drin outlet. Heavy fishing has pushed it to the verge of extinction, and it even appears on the Macedonian 2-denar coin.

hints.habitat: Open water of a large lake, spawning in the shallower shore zones
hints.size: Up to about 76 cm long
hints.diet: Zooplankton when young; adults also hunt small fish

softmouth-trout.funFact: It is easy to spot by its long snout and small, fleshy mouth, and its mostly green body is dotted with red and black spots.
softmouth-trout.revealFact: It lives in just a handful of karst rivers draining to the Adriatic in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro, including the Jadro, Vrljika, Neretva and Zeta. Dams, hybridization with introduced trout and overfishing threaten it.

hints.habitat: Deep, quiet spots in cold streams and small rivers
hints.size: Up to about 70 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Invertebrates

asprete.funFact: Considered a living fossil unchanged for tens of millions of years, it hides under stones by day and fiercely guards its territory at night.
asprete.revealFact: It now survives only in a short stretch of the Vâlsan River in southern Romania, making it the European fish genus with the most restricted range. Surveys in October 2022 confirmed just 58 individuals.

hints.habitat: Under stones in fast, cold, clear mountain streams
hints.size: Up to about 11 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Larvae of stream insects such as mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies

carpione.funFact: It spawns beside underwater springs deep in its lake, and even the oldest individuals live only about five years.
carpione.revealFact: It is endemic to Lake Garda in northern Italy; every attempt to establish it in other lakes has failed, and its numbers fell by about 80% in the ten years up to 2006.

hints.habitat: Deep water of a large lake, spawning near underwater springs
hints.size: Up to about 50 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Zooplankton, plus bottom-dwelling crustaceans and other invertebrates in summer

gwyniad.funFact: It commutes up and down the water column every day, rising toward the surface to forage during the warmer months.
gwyniad.revealFact: The gwyniad, or Welsh whitefish, is native only to Llyn Tegid (Bala Lake) in north Wales, where introduced ruffe eat its eggs and fry. Between 2003 and 2007, eggs were moved to nearby Llyn Arenig Fawr to start a backup population.

hints.habitat: Open water in the deeper parts of a lake; spawns in shallow bays over stones and gravel
hints.size: Up to about 35 cm long (standard length)
hints.diet: Crustaceans and insects

angelshark.funFact: It lies buried in sand by day with only its eyes poking out, and one was once found to have swallowed a cormorant.
angelshark.revealFact: Once widespread from Norway to north-west Africa and the Mediterranean, it is now found mainly around the Canary Islands, with scattered records off Wales and Ireland. Bycatch from intense commercial fishing has made it critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Sand or mud sea floor near the coast and across the continental shelf
hints.size: Up to about 183 cm (1.8 m) long
hints.diet: Mainly flatfish and other bottom fish, plus skates, crustaceans and molluscs

maltese-skate.funFact: This skate wears a set of fake eyes: brown, yellow-centred eye-spots on its wings that may fool or deter predators. Its tail even carries small electric organs, used mainly for communication.
maltese-skate.revealFact: The Maltese skate is one of three rare skates found only in the Mediterranean, living mainly in the Strait of Sicily around Malta, Tunisia and southern Sicily. Because it lives on the seafloor it is often caught by accident in commercial fishing, and this bycatch has left it Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Soft sandy and muddy seabed in deep water, where it can bury itself
hints.size: Up to about 52 cm total length
hints.diet: Crustaceans, mainly amphipods

dalmatian-barbelgudgeon.funFact: Females of this night-active fish have a special egg-laying tube for tucking their eggs into cracks in rock and gravel. In winter or dry spells, adults slip away into underground waters.
dalmatian-barbelgudgeon.revealFact: The Dalmatian barbelgudgeon lives only in karst rivers, lakes and poljes of Dalmatia in Croatia and south-western Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as the Krka and Cetina. Dams, water extraction for farming and pollution threaten it, and it may already be gone from the Zrmanja River.

hints.habitat: Swift streams, still waters and lakes, retreating into underground waters in dry seasons
hints.size: Up to about 20 cm standard length
hints.diet: Omnivorous

apron.funFact: This little perch lurks on stony riverbeds by day and comes out around dusk and at night to feed. Its eggs are so sticky they glue themselves to the gravel, hatching about two weeks later.
apron.revealFact: The apron survives in only a few rivers of the Rhône basin in France and Switzerland, including the Durance, Beaume and Doubs, where the Doubs population may be just 80–160 fish. Dams and water pollution have broken up and degraded its habitat, leaving it Endangered.

hints.habitat: Stony and gravelly riffles in the main channels of fast-flowing rivers
hints.size: Up to about 22 cm total length
hints.diet: Small insects (flies, mayflies, caddisflies) and other aquatic invertebrates

lez-sculpin.funFact: This tiny sculpin was only confirmed as its own species in 2005, after long being lumped with its close cousin, the bullhead. In lab tests, females could lay a new clutch of large eggs within a month of the last.
lez-sculpin.revealFact: The Lez sculpin lives only in a roughly 3 km stretch of the Lez River near Montpellier in southern France. The karstic springs feeding the river may have let this isolated population survive through geological history, but habitat loss now threatens it.

hints.habitat: A short stretch of cold, spring-fed stream
hints.size: Up to about 6.4 cm standard length

knysna-seahorse.funFact: This seahorse's colour shifts with its surroundings and even its mood, from pale green to purplish black. And it's dad who carries the eggs, in a brood pouch under his tail.
knysna-seahorse.revealFact: The Knysna seahorse is known from only three estuaries on South Africa's southern Cape coast: the Knysna Lagoon, Swartvlei and the Keurbooms. Such a tiny range puts it at great risk, and floods in 2007 and 2011 shrank the Keurbooms population.

hints.habitat: Dense seagrass and weed beds in brackish estuaries and lagoons
hints.size: Up to about 12 cm tall (crown to tip of the straightened tail)

pindu.funFact: This jet-black cichlid is reportedly a crab thief, stealing food from freshwater crabs. After spawning, mum keeps the eggs safe in her mouth for three to four weeks.
pindu.revealFact: The pindu lives only in Barombi Mbo, a volcanic crater lake about 3 miles across in western Cameroon. Pollution, sedimentation and water abstraction for the growing town of Kumba threaten it, though commercial fishing on the lake is banned.

hints.habitat: A small volcanic crater lake where only the upper waters hold enough oxygen
hints.size: Up to about 9.1 cm standard length
hints.depth: Within the top 40 m or so (deeper water lacks oxygen)
hints.diet: Shrimp and insect larvae; also steals food from crabs

pungu.funFact: The pungu has a taste for sponge: besides insect larvae, it nibbles a freshwater sponge found nowhere else. Mums brood their eggs in their mouths.
pungu.revealFact: The pungu is endemic to Lake Barombi Mbo in Cameroon, which is also home to three other equally threatened cichlid genera found nowhere else. It is the only member of its genus, named after the Barombi people's own word for the fish, and is threatened by pollution and sedimentation.

hints.habitat: Shallow shoreline waters of a small lake, in small groups
hints.size: Up to about 10 cm standard length
hints.diet: Insect larvae, freshwater sponge, diatoms and plant matter

golden-cave-catfish.funFact: This pale, air-breathing catfish has tiny skin-covered eyes and is probably blind. Its menu includes bat droppings and any unlucky insects that fall into its underground lake.
golden-cave-catfish.revealFact: The golden cave catfish lives only in the lake inside Aigamas Cave in the Otjozondjupa region of Namibia, with an estimated 200–400 individuals. It is the only known cavefish of mainland southern Africa, and water extraction has already lowered its lake.

hints.habitat: A clear lake deep inside a cave
hints.size: Up to about 16 cm standard length
hints.diet: Bat droppings, carcasses, insects and detritus that fall into the water

lake-magadi-tilapia.funFact: Most fish get rid of waste as ammonia, but this cichlid excretes urea instead, because ammonia struggles to diffuse away in highly alkaline water. It can also cope with water as hot as 42 °C!
lake-magadi-tilapia.revealFact: This cichlid is the only fish living in Kenya's hot, hypersaline and highly alkaline Lake Magadi, where it sticks to the springs and lagoons around the shore. It has been introduced to Lakes Elmenteita and Nakuru, but does not seem to have become established in Tanzania's Lake Natron.

hints.habitat: Hot, highly alkaline springs and lagoons around the edge of a very salty lake
hints.size: Up to about 20 cm standard length
hints.diet: Blue-green algae, copepods and fly larvae, taken at the surface

maloti-minnow.funFact: Despite its common name, this little fish isn't a true minnow at all. Youngsters gather in shoals in big pools, while adults prefer going solo or in small groups.
maloti-minnow.revealFact: The Maloti minnow is Lesotho's only endemic freshwater fish, living in upper tributaries of the Senqu (Orange) River in the Maloti–Drakensberg highlands. Invasive fish such as the smallmouth yellowfish threaten it.

hints.habitat: Pools and riffles of clear streams with cobbles and pebbles
hints.size: Up to about 13 cm standard length
hints.diet: Aquatic insects

clanwilliam-sandfish.funFact: This fish rolls and twists so much as it feeds that, in clear water, it is often seen only as a flash of silver. In spring and summer, big crowds migrate upstream together to breed.
clanwilliam-sandfish.revealFact: The Clanwilliam sandfish is found only in the Olifants–Doring River system of South Africa's Western and Northern Cape. It is one of South Africa's most threatened freshwater fish.

hints.habitat: Pools and deep runs in a river's main channel and larger tributaries
hints.size: Up to about 35.5 cm standard length
hints.diet: Algae, detritus and small invertebrates, grazed off rocks or grubbed from soft sediment

red-steenbras.funFact: Both halves of its scientific name point to its favourite hangout: the genus name comes from a word for 'rock', and the species name means 'dweller in rocks'. It is also the biggest member of the whole seabream family.
red-steenbras.revealFact: The red steenbras is found only off South Africa, from Table Bay in the Western Cape to St Lucia in KwaZulu-Natal. Slow to mature at around 7 years old, it has been badly depleted by overfishing.

hints.habitat: Rocky reefs and banks in coastal waters; adults offshore, juveniles on shallower reefs
hints.size: Up to about 200 cm (2 m) total length
hints.diet: Octopuses, crabs and fish

dageraad.funFact: Its scientific name means 'crown-head', a nod to the raised nape of adult males. When cold water wells up, these red reef fish leave their usual home patch, apparently chasing warmer water.
dageraad.revealFact: The dageraad lives only off South Africa, between False Bay in the Western Cape and Durban in KwaZulu-Natal. Long-lived, slow-growing, late to mature and territorial, it was hit hard by overfishing and is now Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Offshore rocky reefs; juveniles on shallower subtidal reefs
hints.size: Up to about 75 cm total length
hints.diet: Crustaceans, molluscs, worms and small fish

lake-chala-tilapia.funFact: This tilapia is the official reference species for its entire genus. Until people introduced other tilapias, it had its home waters all to itself.
lake-chala-tilapia.revealFact: The Lake Chala tilapia is found only in Lake Chala, a small crater lake on the Kenya–Tanzania border at the foot of Kilimanjaro. Siltation and introduced non-native tilapias have made it much rarer, and it is now Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: A small crater lake, often in fairly deep water; feeds among rocks near the shore
hints.size: Up to about 30 cm standard length
hints.diet: Algae and debris picked off the bottom between rocks

saulosi.funFact: These cichlids are all born yellow, but dominant males turn blue with black bars. Some young males stay 'undercover' in yellow among the females, ready to colour up if the boss leaves.
saulosi.revealFact: Pseudotropheus saulosi lives only on Taiwan Reef (Taiwanee Reef) near Chizumulu Island in Lake Malawi. Critically Endangered in the wild, it is being restocked there with captive-bred fish.

hints.habitat: Clean, sediment-free rocks on the upper part of a rocky reef with strong current, in large groups
hints.size: Up to about 8.6 cm total length
hints.diet: Picks and nibbles loose material from the growth coating the rocks

natal-shyshark.funFact: This shark goes by the cheerful nickname 'happy chappie'. It was only described as a species of its own in 2006, having long been treated as a form of a look-alike cousin.
natal-shyshark.revealFact: The Natal shyshark is endemic to a small stretch of South African coast, mainly off KwaZulu-Natal, living in warm water from the surf zone to shallow rocky reefs. Rare and threatened by habitat degradation and commercial fishing, it is assessed as Vulnerable.

hints.habitat: The surf zone and shallow rocky reefs near the coast, living on the bottom

pinstripe-damba.funFact: This cichlid was once listed as extinct in the wild, until a small surviving population was rediscovered. Its body is very flat from side to side and striped with darker vertical bands.
pinstripe-damba.revealFact: The pinstripe damba lives in floodplain lakes of the Sofia River system in north-western Madagascar, where a remnant population was found in Lake Tseny. Invasive species and overfishing threaten it, and zoos and fishkeepers are breeding it in captivity.

hints.habitat: Floodplain lakes of a river system
hints.size: Up to about 16.7 cm standard length

damba-mipentina.funFact: This deep-bodied cichlid is easy to tell apart from its relatives by one big black spot on its side. Zoos and home fishkeepers are breeding it to help the species survive.
damba-mipentina.revealFact: The damba mipentina comes from turbid, shallow floodplain lakes in the Betsiboka and Ikopa River basins of north-western Madagascar. Habitat loss, overfishing and invasive species have caused a drastic decline, leaving it Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Murky, shallow floodplain lakes
hints.size: Up to about 14.8 cm standard length

mangarahara-cichlid.funFact: Its local name means 'red girl', after the males' long, ragged, red-edged fins. When the last known female was killed during a breeding attempt, a media appeal went out to find any survivors.
mangarahara-cichlid.revealFact: The Mangarahara cichlid comes from the Mangarahara and Amboaboa rivers near Mandritsara in northern Madagascar. Feared lost from the wild, a remnant population was found in 2013, and breeding programmes in Madagascar and at Toronto Zoo have since produced thousands of hatchlings.

hints.habitat: A couple of rivers in a very small area, shared with introduced fish
hints.size: Up to about 24.5 cm total length

malagasy-blind-gudgeon.funFact: This blind, pigment-free cavefish is drawn to disturbances on the water's surface. Populations in caves that don't connect to each other may even turn out to be separate species.
malagasy-blind-gudgeon.revealFact: This gudgeon lives only in underground waters of the Mahafaly Plateau in south-western Madagascar, known from more than 10 caves and sinkholes. Some of its caves, including the Mitoho Grotto, are protected within Tsimanampetsotsa National Park.

hints.habitat: Underground water in limestone caves, sinkholes and wells
hints.size: Up to about 8 cm standard length
hints.diet: Crustaceans and insects found in caves

red-tailed-silverside.funFact: Breeding males sport a red spot on the lower jaw, a handy way to tell them from a near-identical cousin that is common in the aquarium trade. The species is named after the pharmacist who collected the first specimen.
red-tailed-silverside.revealFact: The red-tailed silverside lives only in the Mananjary River drainage of eastern Madagascar. It hasn't been found in the lower-lying parts of the basin, probably because deforestation made the water siltier and warmer, and introduced species add to its troubles.

hints.habitat: Shady, quiet stretches of small streams at 300–650 m elevation
hints.size: Up to about 9 cm total length

madagascar-rainbowfish.funFact: These rainbowfish hang out in loose, size-sorted groups of up to several dozen, with youngsters in the shallows and grown-ups in deeper water. Their genus is named after a museum director, Maurice Bedot.
madagascar-rainbowfish.revealFact: Bedotia madagascariensis is found only in eastern Madagascar, in rivers and lakes between the Ivoloina River and Manambolo Creek around Toamasina. Like every member of its family it is endemic to Madagascar, and it is threatened by habitat loss.

hints.habitat: Clear, well-shaded, slow-flowing lowland streams (below about 30 m elevation)
hints.size: Up to about 8.6 cm standard length

sakaramy-killifish.funFact: Unlike some of its relatives, this killifish is not a 'seasonal' species. It lives in mountain brooks and has also been reported from several crater lakes.
sakaramy-killifish.revealFact: Pachypanchax sakaramyi is known only from the Sakaramy and Antongombato rivers, which drain Montagne d'Ambre in northern Madagascar, with reports from several crater lakes. Habitat loss and invasive species threaten it.

hints.habitat: Brooks in mountainous country, and possibly crater lakes
hints.size: Up to about 9 cm total length

patricias-pachypanchax.funFact: This tiny killifish has to watch out not only for fish-eating birds but also for dragonfly nymphs. It is named after a conservationist who ran a charity called Friends of Fishes.
patricias-pachypanchax.revealFact: Patricia's pachypanchax lives in the Mananjeba, Mahavavy du Nord, Ifasy, Manehoko and Ampandra river basins of north-western Madagascar. It honours conservationist Patricia Yazgi, and introduced alien fishes may threaten it in some areas.

hints.habitat: Small tea-coloured, acidic, soft-water rivers, and larger seasonal rivers with floodplains
hints.size: Up to about 5.2 cm standard length
hints.diet: Land and aquatic insects

beluga.funFact: This giant sturgeon rivals the ocean sunfish as the most massive bony fish alive. As it grows, its mouth shifts from underneath its head to almost the front, and its bony scutes are slowly absorbed.
beluga.revealFact: The beluga lives mainly in the Caspian and Black Sea basins, migrating up rivers such as the Volga and Ural to spawn, and was formerly found in the Adriatic. Overfishing and poaching for its roe have crashed wild numbers, and it is Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Open sea, migrating up large, deep, fast rivers to spawn on stone or gravel
hints.size: Up to about 800 cm (8 m) total length
hints.diet: Mostly fish, plus crustaceans and molluscs

tawi-atair-garra.funFact: This pale cavefish lacks pigment, yet surprisingly it has normal eyes, unlike the cave-dwelling form of a close relative.
tawi-atair-garra.revealFact: Garra dunsirei is found only in pools near Tawi Atair, a giant limestone sinkhole in the Dhofar mountains of southern Oman. Confined to this one extremely isolated sinkhole, it is listed as Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Pools in an extremely isolated sinkhole
hints.size: Up to about 6.8 cm standard length

dead-sea-garra.funFact: This small fish is almost a pure algae-grazer. It spawns in groups, releasing eggs into open water that quickly sink to the bottom.
dead-sea-garra.revealFact: The Dead Sea garra lives in springs and wadis draining into the southern Dead Sea in Jordan, such as Wadi Hasa and Ghor Fifa. It once also occurred in Israel but is no longer found there, and habitat loss threatens it.

hints.habitat: Small, fast-running spring-fed streams over gravel
hints.size: Up to about 10 cm standard length
hints.diet: Almost entirely algae

azraq-killifish.funFact: This little toothcarp was feared extinct in the mid-1990s, until a survey in 2000 found about 45 adults hanging on. A captive-breeding rescue mission began the very next year.
azraq-killifish.revealFact: The Azraq killifish lives only in the Azraq Wetland Reserve, an oasis in eastern Jordan. Its survival depends on water levels that are now artificially maintained against illegal water extraction, and on getting rid of the invasive mango tilapia.

hints.habitat: Shallow wetland pools among plants and stones, or over mud
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm total length
hints.diet: Insect larvae and crustaceans

amu-darya-shovelnose.funFact: This small sturgeon trails a long, thin filament from its tail. It comes in two versions: a large, pale form that matures late and a small, dark one that matures early.
amu-darya-shovelnose.revealFact: The Amu Darya shovelnose survives in the middle and lower Amu Darya and the lower Vakhsh River in Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, though it once reached the river's delta in the Aral Sea. Habitat loss, pollution and poaching have made it Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Shallow, turbid, muddy flowing water in a large river
hints.size: Up to about 75 cm total length
hints.diet: Small fish and aquatic insect larvae

persian-sturgeon.funFact: This bluish sturgeon finds food by touch and taste, then simply sucks it in. Its menu grows up with it: tiny shrimp and insect larvae when young, crabs and fish later on.
persian-sturgeon.revealFact: The Persian sturgeon lives mainly in the southern and middle Caspian Sea, spawning in rivers such as the Volga, Kura, Araks and Ural. Overfishing of immature fish, dams, lost spawning grounds and pollution have made it Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Coastal and estuary waters of a sea, running up big, fast rivers to breed
hints.size: Up to about 255 cm (2.5 m) total length
hints.diet: Shrimp, midge larvae and amphipods when young; crabs, then mainly fish, as it grows

mangar.funFact: Artworks more than 3,000 years old show priests or gods dressed in the skin of this giant barbel. Its toothless mouth doesn't hold it back: it eats everything from plankton to birds.
mangar.revealFact: The mangar is native to the Tigris–Euphrates river system in Turkey, Syria, Iraq and Iran, and was already well known in ancient times, appearing in Assyrian art. Overfishing and habitat loss have made it Vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Large rivers and reservoirs, moving into smaller inflows to spawn
hints.size: Up to about 230 cm (2.3 m) total length
hints.diet: Fish (about half its diet), plus zooplankton, invertebrates, phytoplankton and even birds

pearl-mullet.funFact: Each spring this fish heads upstream to spawn, leaping through the air like a salmon. It was long thought to be the only fish in its salty, alkaline home, until a second species was discovered there in 2018.
pearl-mullet.revealFact: The pearl mullet is found only in the Lake Van basin of eastern Turkey, a salty, alkaline soda lake that most fish can't survive in. Heavy catches during its spawning run have become big business, though its IUCN status improved from Endangered in 1994 to Near Threatened in 2014.

hints.habitat: A salty, alkaline lake, plus the freshwater streams it runs up to spawn
hints.size: Up to about 28 cm total length

binni.funFact: This barbel is almost entirely vegetarian; the few tiny animals found in its stomach were probably swallowed by accident. It once sat in a catch-all 'wastebasket' genus before getting a genus all to itself.
binni.revealFact: The binni lives in the lower Tigris–Euphrates basin and the Mesopotamian Marshes of Iraq and south-western Iran, and is highly valued by the Marsh Arabs. Iraq's Umm al Binni Lake was named after it, but draining of the marshes and overfishing have cut its numbers.

hints.habitat: Densely vegetated lakes and marshes, sometimes moving into rivers
hints.size: Up to about 43 cm total length
hints.diet: Plants, from phytoplankton and algae to larger water plants

galilee-tristramella.funFact: This cichlid is the last surviving member of its genus; all the others are extinct. Each fish can spawn at least two or three times in a single breeding season.
galilee-tristramella.revealFact: The short-jaw tristramella lives in the Jordan River system, including Lake Kinneret (the Sea of Galilee), in Israel and Syria. Catches in the lake dropped sharply after 2005, and water extraction and a drying climate threaten it.

hints.habitat: Still or slow water in a river system and a large lake; adults school in open water, young stay near shore
hints.size: Up to about 25 cm total length
hints.diet: Phytoplankton and water plants, plus some zooplankton and small invertebrates

halavi-guitarfish.funFact: Its yellow-grey colouring helps this ray blend in on the seafloor. Mothers give birth to litters of up to 10 pups, each already around 29 cm long.
halavi-guitarfish.revealFact: The halavi guitarfish lives in coastal waters from the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden east to the Gulf of Oman, with just two records (1997 and 2004) in Levantine waters of the Mediterranean. Taken both as a target and as bycatch in small-scale fisheries, it is Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: On the bottom in very shallow coastal water and out over the continental shelf
hints.size: Up to about 120 cm disc width; at least 171 cm total length
hints.diet: Small molluscs, bony fish and crustaceans

ili-marinka.funFact: Each spring this fish pushes into tributary streams, and it spawns over stony bottoms from May until the middle of July.
ili-marinka.revealFact: The Ili marinka is a Schizothorax of Central Asia, found in rivers of the Ili–Balkhash basin in south-eastern Kazakhstan and western China. It is assessed as Vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Rivers and their tributaries, spawning over stony bottoms
hints.size: Up to about 70 cm total length

denisons-barb.funFact: This torpedo-shaped barb, with a red stripe running through its eye, won third prize at a world ornamental-fish show in 1997. It became so popular that collecting for aquariums turned into its biggest threat.
denisons-barb.revealFact: Denison's barb is endemic to fast hill streams of the Western Ghats in southern India, in rivers such as the Chaliyar, Pamba, Achankovil and Valapattanam. By 2007–08 it made up roughly 60–65% of India's live ornamental-fish exports, and over-collection has left it Endangered.

hints.habitat: Rocky pools of fast-flowing hill streams with thick vegetation along the banks
hints.size: Up to about 15 cm total length
hints.diet: Mainly plants (herbivorous)

gollum-snakehead.funFact: This eel-like snakehead lives in underground water yet, unusually, has normal eyes and full colour. One specimen only came to light when a well suddenly turned muddy and was drained for cleaning.
gollum-snakehead.revealFact: The Gollum snakehead lives in underground aquifers of Kerala in south-western India, known from a flooded paddy field at Oorakam and a well about 250 km to the south. It stayed unknown to science until 2018, and an estimated six million groundwater wells in the region threaten it by lowering the water table.

hints.habitat: Warm groundwater aquifers, occasionally turning up in flooded paddy fields and wells
hints.size: Up to about 12.7 cm standard length
hints.diet: Predatory; probably small invertebrates such as insects and crustaceans

hump-backed-mahseer.funFact: For years this huge, orange-tailed mahseer had no proper scientific name, which made it hard to protect. A 2018 study finally matched it to a little-known species described from just 19 fish.
hump-backed-mahseer.revealFact: The hump-backed mahseer is found only in the Kaveri (Cauvery) river basin of the Western Ghats in southern India, in rivers such as the Moyar, Kabini, Bhavani and Pambar. Introduced non-native mahseers, dams and dynamite fishing helped crash its populations around 2004.

hints.habitat: Big rivers, from fast shallow rapids to deep slow pools over bedrock and boulders
hints.size: Up to about 175 cm (1.75 m) fork length

cherry-barb.funFact: Males of this tiny barb turn a deep red when ready to breed. Since 2023 it has had a genus all to itself, Rohanella, named in honour of a biologist.
cherry-barb.revealFact: The cherry barb is endemic to the shaded streams of Sri Lanka's south-western wet zone, from the Kelani to the Nilwala basins. Though widely bred for aquariums, wild populations are still threatened by over-collection and habitat loss.

hints.habitat: Shallow, slow, heavily shaded streams with silt and leaf litter
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm total length
hints.diet: Omnivorous: detritus, algae, diatoms, flies and other small animals

ornate-paradisefish.funFact: This tiny gourami builds a nest out of bubbles, and in aquariums it is said to be exceedingly shy. Its scientific name honours a lawyer and judge.
ornate-paradisefish.revealFact: The ornate paradisefish is endemic to Sri Lanka, living in forest streams of the south-western wet zone. It is the only recognised species in its genus and is listed as Endangered.

hints.habitat: Small, shallow, slow, silty streams in shaded forest, with leaf litter and thick plants along the edges
hints.size: Up to about 4 cm total length
hints.diet: Fish fry, plankton and insect larvae

zebra-loach.funFact: The scientist who first described it couldn't hide his admiration, calling its broad dark and narrow yellow bands 'most beautiful'. Some individuals even wear twisted or net-like stripes.
zebra-loach.revealFact: The zebra loach lives in just four rivers of the northern Western Ghats in India: the Tunga and Bhadra in Karnataka and the Panchganga and Koyna in Maharashtra, an area of about 400 km². Deforestation, pollution and heavy export for the aquarium trade threaten it.

hints.habitat: Clear mountain streams with pebble or gravel beds
hints.size: Up to about 7.8 cm standard length
hints.diet: Omnivorous: phytoplankton and crustaceans from the streambed

pearly-rasbora.funFact: This tiny 'fire rasbora' feeds mainly on land insects such as flies and beetles. In 2018, scientists concluded that a supposedly separate species was really just this fish under another name.
pearly-rasbora.revealFact: The pearly rasbora is endemic to Sri Lanka, where it is restricted to the Kalu River basin in the shaded forest streams of the south-western wet zone. It is more threatened than its relatively widespread relative Rasboroides pallidus.

hints.habitat: Cool, clear, quiet and heavily shaded forest streams with silt and leaf litter
hints.size: Up to about 4 cm total length
hints.diet: Land insects such as flies and beetles, plus detritus

asoka-barb.funFact: Young fish of this barb gather in schools of 30–100 in water just 5–25 cm deep, while the adults move upstream into deeper water. They swim so fast they are hard to identify from above.
asoka-barb.revealFact: The Asoka barb is endemic to Sri Lanka, found only in the upper Sitawaka River and its tributaries and in the Kelani near Kitulgala. Intensive collection by fish exporters has driven its numbers down, and it is Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: Unshaded, fast-flowing river stretches over gravel or sand
hints.size: Up to about 17 cm total length

tambraparni-barb.funFact: This barb was first described in 1953 as a mere subspecies of another barb, before being treated as a full species and moved to a newer genus. Sadly, its numbers have dropped sharply, partly due to sand mining.
tambraparni-barb.revealFact: Dawkinsia tambraparniei is found only in the Tamiraparani (Tambraparni) River basin of the southern Western Ghats in Tamil Nadu, India. Human activities such as sand mining have caused its population to fall significantly in recent years.

hints.habitat: A single river system, where sand mining is a threat
hints.size: Up to about 12.8 cm standard length

black-ruby-barb.funFact: Breeding males turn from silver to deep ruby red, with a jet-black dorsal fin and purple pelvic fins. Their eggs hatch in a day or two, and the fry swim freely just 24 hours later.
black-ruby-barb.revealFact: The black ruby barb is endemic to forested hill streams of south-western Sri Lanka, from the Kelani to the Nilwala basins. A brightly coloured introduced population at Ginigathena is said to have shrunk because of the aquarium export trade.

hints.habitat: Clear, cool, shady forest streams over gravel or sand
hints.size: Up to about 6 cm total length
hints.diet: Mainly filamentous algae and detritus

banggai-cardinalfish.funFact: Dad broods the eggs in his mouth, and the babies stay there even after hatching, with no drifting larval stage at all. Groups hover over sea urchins and duck between the spines when danger looms.
banggai-cardinalfish.revealFact: The Banggai cardinalfish is naturally restricted to the shallows of the Banggai Archipelago off Central Sulawesi, Indonesia, where an estimated 2.4 million fish share about 5,500 km². Heavy collection for the aquarium trade and disease have made it Endangered.

hints.habitat: Calm, shallow seagrass beds, coral reefs and sand, often among long-spined sea urchins
hints.size: Up to about 8 cm total length
hints.diet: Probably small crustaceans from the bottom and the plankton

mekong-giant-catfish.funFact: Young giant catfish have whiskers and teeth, but lose both by the time they are 30–50 cm long. Then they grow astonishingly fast, reaching 150–200 kg in just six years.
mekong-giant-catfish.revealFact: The Mekong giant catfish once ranged along almost the entire Mekong, from Vietnam to China's Yunnan, but now survives only in small, isolated populations in the middle Mekong and Cambodia's Tonlé Sap. Overfishing and habitat loss have made it Critically Endangered.

hints.habitat: The deep main channel of a very large river
hints.size: Up to about 300 cm (3 m) total length (unconfirmed)
hints.diet: Algae and detritus as adults; zooplankton as fry

cave-angelfish.funFact: This eyeless little loach climbs waterfalls, gripping the rock with its fins. In 2016 scientists reported that it walks with a gait like a four-legged animal, thanks to a sturdy hip girdle joined to its spine.
cave-angelfish.revealFact: The cave angelfish is known from eight caves in the Pang Mapha karst of Mae Hong Son Province, northern Thailand, occupying only about 6 km². Agricultural pollution, deforestation and caving tourism threaten its fragile cave streams.

hints.habitat: Swift water over rock, deep inside caves
hints.size: Up to about 2.8 cm standard length
hints.diet: Cave microorganisms and organic matter

giant-barb.funFact: This gentle giant, the largest member of the carp family, has four copies of every chromosome instead of the usual two. It feeds on algae and the fruit of flooded plants rather than chasing prey.
giant-barb.revealFact: The giant barb is found only in the Mekong, Chao Phraya and Mae Klong basins of Indochina, and has vanished entirely from the Chao Phraya River. In Cambodia the catch fell from 200 tonnes in 1964 to just 10 fish in 2000, and the country made it its national fish in 2005.

hints.habitat: Large pools in big rivers, seasonally entering canals, floodplains and flooded forest
hints.size: Up to about 300 cm (3 m) total length (unconfirmed)
hints.diet: Algae, phytoplankton, fruit of flooded plants and detritus

siamese-tiger-perch.funFact: Rounded lobes on its rear fins make this fish look as if it has three tails. Its scientific name means 'beautiful', probably a nod to the bold bars on its orange-brown body.
siamese-tiger-perch.revealFact: The Siamese tiger perch lives in the middle and lower Mekong in Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, including Tonlé Sap, but has been locally extinct in Thailand since the 1990s. Collection for the aquarium trade and damming of its rivers have caused drastic declines.

hints.habitat: Main rivers, tributaries and connected lakes and marshes, around sunken wood and rocky crevices
hints.size: Up to about 40 cm standard length
hints.diet: Fish and shrimp

red-tailed-black-shark.funFact: Despite its name, this 'shark' is really a relative of carp, named for its shark-like looks and moves. Its bright red tail can fade when the fish is stressed, sick or living in poor water.
red-tailed-black-shark.revealFact: The red-tailed black shark is native only to the Chao Phraya River basin of central Thailand, where it is Critically Endangered in the wild. It remains common in aquariums, but every fish in the trade today is captive bred.

hints.habitat: Main river channels and floodplains
hints.size: Up to about 13 cm total length
hints.diet: Omnivorous: plant matter and small bottom-dwelling animals

sawbwa-barb.funFact: This tiny fish has no scales at all. Mature males shimmer silvery blue, set off by a red snout and red tail-fin lobes.
sawbwa-barb.revealFact: The sawbwa barb is endemic to Inle Lake and its surrounding wetlands in Shan State, Myanmar, where it is extremely common. Even so, it is listed as Endangered.

hints.habitat: Large shoals among dense plants in a lake and its swamps, in clear or peaty water
hints.size: Up to about 3 cm long

celestial-pearl-danio.funFact: Its gill covers are see-through, so its blood-red gills shine right through them. Discovered only in 2006, this pearl-spotted mini-fish became an instant hit in the aquarium trade.
celestial-pearl-danio.revealFact: The celestial pearl danio is known only from a tiny area near Hopong, east of Inle Lake in Myanmar, at over 1,000 m elevation in the Salween basin. It lives in spring-fed ponds linked to the Nam Lang and Nam Pawn rivers.

hints.habitat: Tiny, shallow, weedy ponds fed by seeping groundwater or springs, amid open grassland
hints.size: Up to about 2.1 cm standard length
hints.depth: 0–1 m (its ponds are at most about 30 cm deep)

tawilis.funFact: This is the only sardine in its genus known to live entirely in fresh water. It swims with its mouth open to strain plankton, yet still seems to favour the bigger copepods.
tawilis.revealFact: Tawilis lives only in Taal Lake on Luzon in the Philippines, a lake in a volcano's caldera that was cut off from the sea by 18th-century eruptions. It is thought to be one of a few marine species trapped there that evolved into freshwater fish, and overfishing has made it Endangered.

hints.habitat: Open water of a large freshwater lake, schooling just below the surface
hints.size: Up to about 12 cm total length
hints.diet: Plankton, especially larger copepods, plus rotifers and water fleas

black-betta.funFact: Named after Persephone, queen of the Underworld, this tiny betta survives dry spells by burying itself in damp leaf litter. It also builds a ball of bubbles among plants to hold its eggs.
black-betta.revealFact: Betta persephone is known only from Johor in Peninsular Malaysia, with its type locality in the peat swamp forest at Ayer Hitam. Its small swampy range is shrinking as forests are cleared for oil palm plantations.

hints.habitat: Dark, soft, acidic blackwater streams and peat swamps under a closed forest canopy
hints.size: Up to about 2.6 cm standard length
hints.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates

mahachai-betta.funFact: The paper naming this betta was its journal's most-read of 2012, viewed over 15,000 times. Pairs court, build bubble nests and raise fry in tiny pools of water cupped inside palm bracts.
mahachai-betta.revealFact: Named after the Mahachai area of Samut Sakhon, Thailand, this betta lives in brackish nipa-palm swamps west of Bangkok. It is the only Betta known to cope with both fresh and brackish water, and it is considered critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Still water of swamps, pools and ponds among nipa palms, fresh to slightly salty
hints.size: Up to about 4.4 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

indonesian-coelacanth.funFact: Science first learned of this brown lobe-finned fish in 1997, when a honeymooning couple photographed one at a local market. A rival claim of an earlier find hinged on a photo later exposed as a crude forgery.
indonesian-coelacanth.revealFact: First spotted at a market on Manado Tua, North Sulawesi, this coelacanth lives on deep slopes of eastern Indonesia, with populations off Sulawesi, Papua and North Maluku. It is one of only two living coelacanth species and is listed as vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Rocky slopes and caves in deep, cool water
hints.size: Up to about 140 cm (1.4 m) long
hints.depth: About 150–200 m (one pair was seen in a cave at 155 m)

psychedelic-frogfish.funFact: Its swirling stripes act like a fingerprint: every individual's pattern is unique, so researchers can identify each one from any angle. Now and then it stretches its head and mouth wide, as if yawning.
psychedelic-frogfish.revealFact: The psychedelic frogfish has been confirmed only at Ambon Island in Indonesia's Maluku islands, where it hides in coral rubble near a harbour jetty at a dive site known as the 'Twilight Zone'. It was described in 2009 and named for its swirling stripes.

hints.habitat: Coarse coral rubble, crusted with sponges and sea squirts, on a gently sloping harbour floor
hints.size: Up to about 6.5 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

halmahera-walking-shark.funFact: This small shark would rather walk than swim, using its pectoral fins to stroll along the seafloor. Its brown body is dotted with clusters of brown and white spots arranged in polygon shapes.
halmahera-walking-shark.revealFact: Named for Halmahera in Indonesia's North Maluku, this epaulette shark was described from two specimens collected near Ternate island in 2013. Its closest look-alike, from West Papua, has seven large dark spots on each side instead of spot clusters.

hints.habitat: Near-shore coastal waters, where it walks along the sea bottom
hints.size: Up to about 68 cm long

celebes-rainbowfish.funFact: Its slender body is almost completely see-through apart from a blue stripe along each side, while males sport stretched-out black fins. It's the only known species in its genus.
celebes-rainbowfish.revealFact: The Celebes rainbowfish lives only near the town of Maros in South Sulawesi, Indonesia (Celebes is Sulawesi's former name). The ornamental fish trade and pollution have sharply reduced its numbers.

hints.habitat: Well-oxygenated streams and estuaries, fresh to slightly salty, hiding among plant leaves
hints.size: Up to about 8 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Small worms, insects and bits of plant matter

daisys-ricefish.funFact: Fully grown, this ricefish is under 3 cm long without its tail fin, and instead of hugging the bottom it lives up in open water.
daisys-ricefish.revealFact: Daisy's ricefish is known only from streams on Muna Island, off South-east Sulawesi in Indonesia. It is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Freshwater streams, swimming in open water
hints.size: Up to about 2.8 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

kunimasu.funFact: Written off as extinct for about 70 years, this dark, black-spotted salmon turned up alive in 2010, descended from eggs shipped to other lakes in the 1930s. DNA tests later proved it was no hybrid.
kunimasu.revealFact: The kunimasu originally lived only in Lake Tazawa in Akita Prefecture, Japan, until strongly acidic river water diverted in for hydroelectric power killed it off in 1940. It survives today in Lake Saiko near Mount Fuji, where eggs had been sent in 1935.

hints.habitat: Cold, deep water of a freshwater lake
hints.size: Up to about 24 cm long
hints.diet: Probably zooplankton drifting in deep water

kaluga.funFact: One of the biggest sturgeons on Earth, it can reach about 5.6 m, and there are even reports of kalugas tipping over fishing boats. Older fish spawn less often, sometimes waiting four years or more.
kaluga.revealFact: The kaluga lives in the Amur River basin along the Russia–China border, spending part of its life in the salty estuary. Hunted to near extinction for its valuable roe, it is critically endangered, and poaching continues despite constant patrols.

hints.habitat: A huge river system and its estuary; adults live in rivers and lakes and sometimes enter salt water
hints.size: Up to about 560 cm (5.6 m) long
hints.diet: Invertebrates at first, then young fish; adults hunt fish such as salmon

chinese-sturgeon.funFact: It makes the longest migration of any sturgeon, swimming from the coast far upriver to spawn. One female can carry over a million eggs, yet fewer than 1% of the hatchlings survive.
chinese-sturgeon.revealFact: The Chinese sturgeon spawns in the Yangtze River and lives along China's eastern coasts; it once also reached Japan and Korea but has vanished from both. Protected as a 'national treasure' like the giant panda, it is critically endangered by habitat loss and overfishing.

hints.habitat: Coastal seas as adults, migrating far up a large river to spawn; young in slow water
hints.size: Up to about 346 cm (3.5 m) long
hints.diet: Adults eat almost any water animal they can swallow; young eat aquatic insects, larvae and diatoms

high-fin-banded-shark.funFact: Despite being sold as a 'banded shark', this fish is a sucker with no relation to real sharks. It's an 'ugly duckling in reverse': the bold bands of youth vanish as it darkens into adulthood.
high-fin-banded-shark.revealFact: The Chinese high-fin banded shark is native to the Yangtze River basin of China, and its population in the Min River tributary may already be gone. It is listed as vulnerable in the wild, though it is widely farmed.

hints.habitat: Main channels of a large river, moving into fast, shallow headwaters to spawn
hints.size: Up to about 68 cm long

sakhalin-taimen.funFact: One of the largest and most ancient salmon, it takes about eight years to mature and lives roughly fourteen. Once longer than about 30 cm, it eats nothing but other fish.
sakhalin-taimen.revealFact: The Sakhalin taimen lives in rivers and lakes of Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and the Russian Far East mainland, as well as Hokkaido in Japan. Habitat loss, bycatch and poaching have cut it to under 5% of its historic numbers, so it is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Lower and middle reaches of rivers and lakes; some populations head out to sea
hints.size: Up to about 200 cm (2 m) long
hints.diet: Aquatic insects when young; only fish once over about 30 cm

tokyo-bitterling.funFact: Like other bitterlings, it lays its eggs inside freshwater mussel shells, but this one is fussy and uses only one kind of mussel, which limits its breeding chances.
tokyo-bitterling.revealFact: The Tokyo bitterling now survives only on the Kantō Plain around Tokyo, Japan, where people and pollution have overrun its streams. The Japanese government has declared it a 'national monument' to give it special protection.

hints.habitat: Gentle little freshwater streams, where it needs one particular mussel to breed
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm long

ayumodoki.funFact: Also called the kissing loach, it spawns just once a year in flooded rice paddies and ditches, racing to breed in the few days they hold water. Six barbels near its mouth help it feel for food in mud.
ayumodoki.revealFact: The ayumodoki lives only in a few river systems on Honshu, Japan, such as the Yodo River system near Kyoto and the Yoshii River in Okayama, whose rice paddies it uses for spawning. It is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Fast, muddy streams and rivers, moving into flooded rice paddies to spawn
hints.size: Up to about 15 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.depth: Spawns in flooded paddies roughly 54 cm deep
hints.diet: Water fleas when young; later detritus, mud worms and other small bottom animals

qinghai-naked-carp.funFact: This carp is almost scaleless, keeping only a few specialised scales near its vent and shoulders, hence 'naked carp'. It grows slowly, needing 7–10 years before it can breed.
qinghai-naked-carp.revealFact: Przewalski's naked carp lives only in Lake Qinghai and its tributaries on the north-eastern Tibetan Plateau, China's largest saline lake with no outflow. From April to July adults leave the brackish lake and swim up a handful of freshwater rivers to spawn.

hints.habitat: A huge, slightly salty lake with no outlet, plus the slow freshwater streams feeding it
hints.size: Up to about 48 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Mostly zooplankton near the bottom, plus other small aquatic invertebrates

white-cloud-minnow.funFact: Its genus name means 'Tan's fish', after the scout leader who discovered it in the 1930s. It can cope with water as chilly as 5°C, one reason it's a classic beginner's aquarium fish.
white-cloud-minnow.revealFact: The White Cloud Mountain minnow was discovered on White Cloud Mountain in Guangzhou, Guangdong, China, where pollution and tourism have nearly wiped it out. After it was long thought extinct in the wild, an apparently native population was found on Hainan Island.

hints.habitat: Clean, slow-flowing streams thick with water plants
hints.size: Up to about 4 cm long
hints.diet: Zooplankton and detritus, plus plants and insect larvae

hong-kong-grouper.funFact: Its pale grey-brown body is sprinkled with tiny red, orange or gold spots and crossed by six faint dark bars. Divers have reported summer gatherings of up to 50 on reefs, right in spawning season.
hong-kong-grouper.revealFact: The Hong Kong grouper lives on rocky and coral reefs of the western Pacific, from southern Japan and Korea through China and Taiwan to the Gulf of Tonkin. It is endangered and is a familiar sight in Hong Kong's live fish markets.

hints.habitat: Rocky and coral reefs; young ones stay in shallower water
hints.size: Up to about 58 cm long

japanese-angelshark.funFact: A flat, wing-finned ambush hunter, it lies still on the sand all day and strikes at night. Its lineage split from its closest angelshark cousins about 100 million years ago, in the Cretaceous.
japanese-angelshark.revealFact: The Japanese angelshark lives on sandy bottoms of the north-western Pacific off Japan, Korea, China and Taiwan, and its type specimen came from Nagasaki. Caught in large numbers for meat and shagreen leather, it is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Sandy sea bottoms on the continental shelf
hints.size: Up to about 200 cm (2 m) long
hints.diet: Fishes, cephalopods and crustaceans

spotted-handfish.funFact: Its hand-shaped fins let it stroll across the seafloor instead of swimming. Females lay eggs on upright objects such as sea squirts and seagrass, and the young hatch 7–8 weeks later as fully formed mini handfish.
spotted-handfish.revealFact: The spotted handfish lives only in the Derwent Estuary of south-east Tasmania, Australia, and nearby areas. It is critically endangered, chiefly threatened by an invasive species, the Northern Pacific seastar.

hints.habitat: Sandy bottoms in sheltered inshore waters, often in shell-filled hollows
