hints.size: Up to about 15 cm long

red-handfish.funFact: Studded with little warts and dressed in red, it crawls on hand-like fins instead of swimming. Parents stand guard over their clusters of 30–60 eggs until the young hatch.
red-handfish.revealFact: Once found at several sites around south-east Tasmania, the red handfish is now known from just two small reefs in Frederick Henry Bay, each no more than about 50 m across. Its slow breeding and dispersal keep its range tiny, and it is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Rocky reef edges next to sand, hidden under seaweed canopies
hints.size: Up to about 9 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.depth: To about 6 m per FishBase (other records say 1–20 m)
hints.diet: Small bottom-living animals such as crustaceans and polychaete worms

australian-lungfish.funFact: When it gulps air at the surface, its exhale has been likened to the puff of a small bellows. Nearly identical fossils show its genus has barely changed in over 100 million years.
australian-lungfish.revealFact: The Australian lungfish is native only to the Mary and Burnett river systems of south-east Queensland, Australia, though it has been introduced to rivers farther south. It is the last surviving member of its family and is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Deep pools of slow rivers and still water, over mud, sand or gravel
hints.size: Up to about 170 cm (1.7 m) long
hints.diet: Frogs, tadpoles, fish, shrimp, earthworms, snails, water plants and fallen fruit

red-finned-blue-eye.funFact: Only the males of this tiny fish wear red fins. Its pools are just a few centimetres deep and sit in full sun, where air temperatures swing from 3°C in winter to 51°C in summer.
red-finned-blue-eye.revealFact: The red-finned blue-eye lives only in a cluster of artesian springs on Edgbaston Reserve in central Queensland, Australia, and by 2021 was down to one wild spring. Invasive mosquitofish are a major threat, but a 2021 release of captive-bred fish lifted its numbers from about 200 to around 3,000.

hints.habitat: Slightly salty spring-fed pools among grassy tussocks in dry, open country
hints.size: Up to about 2.5 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

canterbury-mudfish.funFact: The first specimen reached scientists by parcel post, packed in a tin box of damp earth, and was still lively after a 30-hour journey. Its name honours the farmer who sent it, not its burrowing habit.
canterbury-mudfish.revealFact: The Canterbury mudfish (kowaro) lives only on the Canterbury Plains of New Zealand's South Island, from just north of Christchurch to the Waitaki River. Its wetlands were largely drained for farming, so it now clings on in springs, water races and drains.

hints.habitat: Wetlands, springs and drains that can dry out over summer
hints.size: Up to about 15 cm long

gollum-galaxias.funFact: This scaleless little fish has big eyes set high on its head, each wider than 23% of its head length. It also packs enlarged canine teeth in both jaws.
gollum-galaxias.revealFact: The Gollum galaxias lives only in southern New Zealand: streams of the Southland Plains, tributaries of the Clutha River, the Catlins and Stewart Island / Rakiura. It belongs to a group of 10 species that were once all lumped together as a single species.

hints.habitat: Slow or still lowland streams and wetlands, among moss, woody debris and plant-lined banks
hints.size: The type specimen measured about 7.5 cm long

blind-cave-eel.funFact: Eyeless and pale pink to white, this eel-like fish was seen only 36 times between 1959 and 2017. Scientists now search for it by testing cave water for traces of its DNA.
blind-cave-eel.revealFact: The blind cave eel lives in underground waters of north-western Australia, in the Cape Range area near Exmouth, the Pilbara and Barrow Island. It is Australia's longest cavefish and one of only three vertebrates there that live solely underground.

hints.habitat: Pitch-dark, slightly salty, tide-influenced water in limestone caves and wells
hints.size: Up to about 40 cm long
hints.diet: Invertebrates such as crustaceans, plus land creatures washed into the caves

salamanderfish.funFact: Its eyes can't move, so this little fish swivels its neck instead. When its pool dries up it burrows into the sand and breathes through its skin until the water returns.
salamanderfish.revealFact: The salamanderfish lives only in acidic pools on peat flats in the far south-west of Western Australia, between the Blackwood and Kent rivers. It is such an isolated lineage that it sits alone in its own superorder, and it is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Shallow, acidic, tea-coloured pools and streams that dry out in summer
hints.size: Up to about 7.4 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.depth: Pools no deeper than about 0.1 m
hints.diet: Mainly aquatic insect larvae and small crustaceans

boesemans-rainbowfish.funFact: This rainbowfish looks like two fish joined at the middle: bluish-grey to purple up front and orange-red at the back. It can dial its colours up or down, a sign of mood or health.
boesemans-rainbowfish.revealFact: Boeseman's rainbowfish lives only in the Ayamaru (Ajamaru) Lakes and their tributaries on the Bird's Head (Vogelkop) Peninsula of West Papua, Indonesia. It is named after Dutch ichthyologist Marinus Boeseman, who collected the first specimens, and is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Mountain lakes at a river's headwaters, and their feeder streams
hints.size: Up to about 9 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Omnivorous; in aquariums it favours meatier foods

kutubu-rainbowfish.funFact: Nicknamed the turquoise rainbowfish, it shares its one home lake with 12 other fish species found nowhere else on Earth.
kutubu-rainbowfish.revealFact: The Lake Kutubu rainbowfish lives only in Lake Kutubu and its outflow in the Southern Highlands of Papua New Guinea, part of the Kikori River system. It is one of 13 fish species endemic to the lake and is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: A highland lake and its outlet stream, far upstream from the sea
hints.size: Up to about 10 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Omnivorous

red-rainbowfish.funFact: Males blaze bright red and grow a taller back with age, though low-ranking males stay drab. Its scientific name is almost always misspelt: grammar demands 'incisa', not 'incisus'.
red-rainbowfish.revealFact: The red rainbowfish is found only in Lake Sentani and its tributaries near Jayapura in Papua, Indonesia. A fast-growing human population around the lake and introduced fish such as tilapia have made it endangered.

hints.habitat: A lake in hilly country about 75 m above sea level, and its tributaries
hints.size: Up to about 12 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Omnivorous, possibly a bit more meat-loving than its relatives

lake-wanam-rainbowfish.funFact: Its whole natural home is one small lake just 2–3 km across, where introduced tilapia have nearly wiped it out. Luckily, captive populations keep the species going.
lake-wanam-rainbowfish.revealFact: The Lake Wanam rainbowfish is endemic to Lake Wanam near Lae in Papua New Guinea. Competition from introduced tilapias has made it critically endangered, and it has virtually vanished from the wild.

hints.habitat: A small lake about 150 m above sea level
hints.size: Up to about 9 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Omnivorous

maugean-skate.funFact: Only discovered in 1988, this skate shows its sex on its tail: males carry three rows of thorns there, females five. The entire population may be fewer than 1,000 fish.
maugean-skate.revealFact: Nicknamed the 'thylacine of the sea', the Maugean skate lives only in brackish estuaries on Tasmania's west coast, mainly Macquarie Harbour, and may be gone from Bathurst Harbour. Salmon farming in Macquarie Harbour could push it to extinction.

hints.habitat: Dim, tannin-stained, brackish estuary channels with silty bottoms
hints.size: Up to about 71 cm long
hints.diet: Bottom-living prey, mostly crustaceans

whites-seahorse.funFact: Here the dads get pregnant: after a three-week gestation a male gives birth to about 150 young, and may do it several times a season. Pairs stay faithful all season, and some even settle on shark nets.
whites-seahorse.revealFact: White's seahorse, also called the Sydney seahorse, lives in estuaries and sheltered bays of central New South Wales, from Port Stephens to the Sydney area. As its natural seagrass and sponge habitats disappear, it increasingly uses jetties and other artificial structures.

hints.habitat: Sheltered bays among seagrass, sponges, soft corals and kelp, and under jetties
hints.size: Up to about 13 cm long
hints.diet: Small crustaceans such as copepods, amphipods, shrimp and mysids

pedder-galaxias.funFact: This galaxias spawns in frigid water of just 6.7–7.5°C, laying up to 1,200 eggs. Its menu ranges from water-insect larvae to land insects like beetles, flies and even cicadas.
pedder-galaxias.revealFact: The Pedder galaxias once lived only in Lake Pedder in south-west Tasmania, but after a 1972 dam created a 'new' Lake Pedder and introduced trout took hold, none has been caught in the wild since 1996. It survives in two translocated populations, including one in Lake Oberon in the Western Arthurs range.

hints.habitat: Rocky edges of a lake with dark, tannin-stained water
hints.size: Up to about 16 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Crustaceans, aquatic insect larvae and land insects such as beetles, flies and cicadas

mccullochs-anemonefish.funFact: Each group is ruled by its biggest fish, the female; if she dies, the breeding male turns female and the next-largest steps up. It lives with just one kind of anemone, the bubble-tip.
mccullochs-anemonefish.revealFact: McCulloch's anemonefish lives only around Lord Howe Island and the nearby Middleton and Elizabeth reefs in the south-western Pacific. Its tiny range and reliance on a single kind of anemone make it vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Lagoons and rocky reefs, always with bubble-tip anemones
hints.size: Up to about 12 cm long

doubleheader-wrasse.funFact: Both males and females grow a big bulging hump on the forehead, which explains its scientific name ('bump-forehead') and its nickname, the doubleheader. It ties for largest wrasse in its genus.
doubleheader-wrasse.revealFact: The doubleheader lives around Lord Howe Island, Norfolk Island and Middleton Reef in the south-west Pacific, only rarely turning up off New South Wales. Usually seen in small groups dominated by one large male, it is listed as vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Shallow rocky and coral reefs; young ones in tide pools
hints.size: Up to about 60 cm long
hints.diet: Snails, clams and other bivalves, and crabs

nopili-rock-climbing-goby.funFact: Within two days, a young goby's mouth shifts from the front of its face to underneath, letting it inch up sheer waterfalls with mouth and belly suckers. Adults tend algae 'gardens' on boulders.
nopili-rock-climbing-goby.revealFact: The nopili rock-climbing goby is endemic to the Hawaiian Islands, living in clear, fast mountain streams on all the main islands, though it is now rare on Oahu. Its larvae drift out to sea, and juveniles must climb back past towering waterfalls to reach upstream pools.

hints.habitat: Fast, rocky mountain streams with clean gravel and no silt
hints.size: Up to about 20 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Diatoms and filamentous algae grazed off rocks

oopu-alamoo.funFact: This little goby scales waterfalls in 'powerbursts', shoving off with its pectoral fins and sticking back on with a belly sucker. It has turned up above a waterfall more than 130 m tall.
oopu-alamoo.revealFact: The ʻoʻopu ʻalamoʻo is endemic to the Hawaiian Islands, living in mountain streams up to about 750 m elevation on Hawaii, Maui, Molokai, Kauai and Oahu. It has even been found above ʻAkaka Falls on the Big Island, which drops more than 130 m.

hints.habitat: Upper reaches of fast mountain streams, above waterfalls
hints.size: Up to about 7 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Algae such as diatoms, grazed from rocks as it climbs

clipperton-angelfish.funFact: In 2009 a dealer tried to smuggle 52 of these angelfish past wildlife officers by declaring them as king angelfish, hoping to sell each for $10,000. Youngsters wear blue bars that fade with age.
clipperton-angelfish.revealFact: The Clipperton angelfish lives only around Clipperton Island, a remote French atoll in the eastern Pacific west of Costa Rica. Its isolation makes it extremely scarce in the aquarium trade, where it fetches very high prices.

hints.habitat: Reef waters around a single remote atoll
hints.size: Up to about 25 cm long

galapagos-grouper.funFact: These groupers appear to start adult life as females and switch to male around age 12. Every so often one shows up entirely bright yellow instead of the usual spotted grey-brown.
galapagos-grouper.revealFact: The Galápagos (sailfin) grouper lives off the Galápagos Islands of Ecuador, with smaller populations at Cocos Island (Costa Rica) and Malpelo Island (Colombia). It is the most valuable finfish landed by the islands' handline fishery and is now endangered.

hints.habitat: Rock walls, lava ridges and drop-offs; young in lagoons, seagrass, mangroves and even inland lava ponds
hints.size: Up to about 120 cm (1.2 m) long
hints.diet: Mainly other fish, especially creolefish

mariana-snailfish.funFact: This pale, tadpole-like fish lives close to about 8,200 m, the apparent depth limit for bony fish. Its skin is see-through, its skull is only partly turned to bone, and it can barely see, if at all.
mariana-snailfish.revealFact: The Mariana snailfish lives in the Mariana Trench of the western Pacific, mostly at 7,000–8,000 m, where it appears to be the top predator. It is named for Herbert Swire of the 1870s Challenger expedition, which found the Challenger Deep.

hints.habitat: The pitch-dark, high-pressure floor of the deep sea
hints.size: Up to about 22.6 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Tiny crustaceans, especially amphipods

african-coelacanth.funFact: Known to science only from fossils until 1938, this 'living fossil' spends its days in caves, sometimes 14 to a cave. At night it drifts out alone to hunt, travelling up to 8 km before heading home by dawn.
african-coelacanth.revealFact: The West Indian Ocean coelacanth lives on deep rocky slopes mainly around the Comoros (Grande Comore and Anjouan), with smaller populations off South Africa, Mozambique, Tanzania, Kenya and Madagascar. The first scientific specimen came from a South African trawler in 1938, and the genus Latimeria honours museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, who spotted it.

hints.habitat: Steep rocky slopes riddled with caves
hints.size: Up to about 168 cm (1.7 m) long
hints.diet: Fishes and squid

st-helena-sharpnose-puffer.funFact: Adults of this little pufferfish are usually seen in pairs. Unlike its close relatives, it has no dark stripes along its body or tail base and no bold dark spot on its back.
st-helena-sharpnose-puffer.revealFact: The St Helena sharpnose pufferfish is known only from the remote South Atlantic islands of St Helena and Ascension. It is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Tide pools and rocky areas around remote islands
hints.size: Up to about 6.7 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

rocas-gregory.funFact: In this little damselfish the dads babysit: males guard the eggs and fan them with fresh water. Pairs team up to breed, and the eggs are stuck to the bottom.
rocas-gregory.revealFact: The Rocas gregory lives only around Rocas Atoll and the Fernando de Noronha archipelago off north-eastern Brazil, and has also been reported from the St Peter and St Paul Archipelago. It is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Shallow outer reefs, lagoons and rock pools, around rocks and rubble
hints.size: Up to about 9 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

noronha-cleaner-goby.funFact: This tiny goby runs a cleaning service, with up to 15 workers at the busiest stations. Its clients span about 30 fish species, including big predators like sharks and groupers.
noronha-cleaner-goby.revealFact: The Noronha cleaner goby lives only on the reefs of the Fernando de Noronha archipelago off north-eastern Brazil. It is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Cleaning stations on coral heads, sponges and rocks around small islets
hints.size: Up to about 3.2 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

golden-panchax.funFact: In breeding season the male's scales lift up, giving his skin a rough look. It was also among the very first killifish kept in aquariums, back in the 1860s.
golden-panchax.revealFact: The golden panchax is the only freshwater fish endemic to the Seychelles, found only on the granitic islands. A population taken to Zanzibar for mosquito control after the First World War lasted for decades before invasive tilapia wiped it out.

hints.habitat: Small fresh and brackish streams, ponds and marshes
hints.size: Up to about 10 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Worms, crustaceans, insects and small fish

greenland-shark.funFact: It may live 272–510 years, longer than any other known vertebrate, and doesn't mature until around age 150. Many carry parasites clamped onto their eyes, yet they get by on smell and hearing.
greenland-shark.revealFact: The Greenland shark roams the cold, deep waters of the Arctic and northern North Atlantic, from Greenland, Iceland and Svalbard to Arctic Canada and northern Norway. Its deep, remote home means it is still poorly studied, and it is listed as vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Frigid shelf and slope waters, usually below 5°C; enters shallow bays in colder months
hints.size: Up to about 427 cm (4.3 m) long
hints.diet: A generalist: many kinds of fish, plus carrion

blackfin-icefish.funFact: It has no haemoglobin at all, so its blood is see-through and its gills are creamy white, a trait found only in icefishes. With no swim bladder, it rests on the seabed on thick-skinned pelvic fins.
blackfin-icefish.revealFact: The blackfin icefish lives around the Scotia Arc in the Southern Ocean: South Georgia, the South Orkney and South Shetland islands, Bouvet Island and the Antarctic Peninsula. The icy, oxygen-rich water there lets it survive without haemoglobin.

hints.habitat: The seabed of near-freezing, oxygen-rich shelf seas
hints.size: Up to about 72 cm long
hints.diet: Mostly fish and krill

bocaccio.funFact: A single female can produce over 2 million eggs a season, releasing her young as live larvae rather than laying eggs. Juveniles hide under floating kelp mats, driftwood and even oil platforms.
bocaccio.revealFact: The bocaccio ranges along the eastern North Pacific from Alaska to central Baja California, and is most abundant from Oregon to northern Baja California. It can live at least 50 years and is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Rocky reefs and open bottoms; young shelter near shore under floating kelp
hints.size: Up to about 91 cm long
hints.diet: Mainly fish, including other rockfish; young eat zooplankton such as copepods

watercress-darter.funFact: True to its name, it perches on watercress leaves and stems well above the stream bed. In 2008 over 12,000 died when workers removed a beaver dam whose pond kept flooding a nearby tennis court.
watercress-darter.revealFact: The watercress darter is known from just four bodies of water in the Black Warrior River basin near Birmingham, Alabama, including the Watercress Darter National Wildlife Refuge. Its tiny range, small population and sensitivity to spring water quality make it endangered.

hints.habitat: Slow, spring-fed water thick with watercress and other plants
hints.size: Up to about 5.4 cm long
hints.diet: Snails, crustaceans and insect larvae

cuban-blind-cusk-eel.funFact: Rather than laying eggs, this cave-dwelling fish gives birth to live young. It shares its dark underground waters with two other members of its genus.
cuban-blind-cusk-eel.revealFact: Lucifuga dentata is endemic to Cuba, where it lives in flooded limestone caves and sinkholes in the west of the island. It is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Dark freshwater in underground caves
hints.size: Up to about 15.2 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Small cave isopods (cirolanids)

humpbacked-limia.funFact: As males age they grow a distinct hump and turn more golden, then woo females by flaring a big purple-flecked dorsal fin and wagging their tails. Mothers give birth to 15–30 live young.
humpbacked-limia.revealFact: The humpbacked limia lives only in Lake Miragoâne in Haiti, which suffers from severe deforestation, pollution and climate change. With no species-specific protection in place, it is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: A lake with weedy, muddy shallows; schools over all kinds of bottoms
hints.size: Up to about 5.2 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Only detritus and algae

sulphur-limia.funFact: Its scientific name means 'sulphur-loving', because the first specimens were caught in a sulphur spring. Mature males flash yellow-to-orange dorsal fins, and bluish-purple scales glint along its sides.
sulphur-limia.revealFact: The sulphur limia is known for certain only from the sulphur spring at Balneario La Zurza, on the south-eastern shore of Lake Enriquillo in the Dominican Republic. It is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: A lowland sulphur spring with hard, alkaline water and a sandy to gravelly bottom
hints.size: Up to about 3.9 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)

highland-splitfin.funFact: Its scientific name is a double tribute, honouring two ichthyologists who teamed up on a 1939 review of its fish family. It's the only species in its genus.
highland-splitfin.revealFact: The highland splitfin is endemic to Mexico's Lerma River basin; it was first described in 1940 from Cointzio, Michoacán, and now survives around Laguna de Zacapu and nearby springs. It is critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Rivers, ponds and springs
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm long

clarion-damselfish.funFact: About 95% of the entire species lives around one small group of islands. As in other damselfish, the dads guard the eggs and keep them aerated.
clarion-damselfish.revealFact: The Clarion damselfish ranges from Mexico's Revillagigedo Islands to the southern tip of Baja California, but about 95% of the population lives around the Revillagigedo Islands. Warm El Niño events could threaten it, and it is listed as vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Rocky inshore reefs
hints.size: Up to about 12 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Omnivorous

iporanga-blind-catfish.funFact: This blind catfish grows less than 1 mm a month but can live 15 to 20 years. It barely shies from light, roaming the whole water column right up to the surface.
iporanga-blind-catfish.revealFact: Pimelodella kronei lives only in cave streams of the Betari River basin in the upper Ribeira de Iguape valley near Iporanga, São Paulo state, Brazil. It was the first cave-dwelling fish ever described from Brazil.

hints.habitat: Underground headwater streams with rocky rapids and soft-bottomed pools
hints.size: Up to about 20 cm long (body length, tail fin excluded)
hints.diet: Invertebrates; an opportunistic carnivore

magnificent-pearlfish.funFact: This little killifish lays its eggs in the bottom, and they take about five months to develop before hatching.
magnificent-pearlfish.revealFact: The magnificent pearlfish lives in seasonal floodplain pools of the middle São Francisco River basin in northern Minas Gerais and Bahia, Brazil. It is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Temporary pools on a river floodplain
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm long

nahuelbuta-velvet-catfish.funFact: This bottom-dwelling fish belongs to the velvet catfishes, family Diplomystidae, and can grow to about 26 cm long.
nahuelbuta-velvet-catfish.revealFact: This velvet catfish is endemic to Chile, where it lives in the Biobío and Imperial river basins and some coastal basins of the Biobío Region, rivers that drain the Nahuelbuta Range. It is listed as endangered.

hints.habitat: Rivers and coastal river basins, living near the bottom
hints.size: Up to about 26 cm long

mountain-catfish.funFact: It's the last living member of its entire family: a scaleless catfish with three pairs of whiskers, sprouting from its chin, its upper jaw and even beside its nostrils.
mountain-catfish.revealFact: This critically endangered catfish lives only in the fresh waters of central Chile. It is the sole surviving species of the family Nematogenyidae, and the only other species described in its genus is extinct.

hints.habitat: On the bottom of freshwater rivers
hints.size: Up to about 41 cm long

irwins-percilia.funFact: A perch-like fish under 10 cm long, it belongs to the family Perciliidae and lives in just two river basins anywhere on Earth.
irwins-percilia.revealFact: Irwin's percilia is found only in the Malleco and Biobío river basins of south-central Chile, and is listed as Endangered.

hints.habitat: Freshwater rivers, between the bottom and midwater
hints.size: Up to about 9.6 cm long

argentine-angelshark.funFact: This flattened shark wears purplish-brown camouflage with dark spots clustered in little rings, and mothers give birth to litters of about 7 to 11 live pups.
argentine-angelshark.revealFact: It lives on the outer continental shelf and upper slope of the south-western Atlantic, from southern Brazil to Patagonia. Its population is very slow to recover, taking more than 14 years to double, which leaves it highly vulnerable.

hints.habitat: On the sea floor of the continental shelf and upper slope
hints.size: Up to about 170 cm (1.7 m) long
hints.diet: Bottom-living fishes, shrimp and squid

patagonian-seahorse.funFact: Dads carry the pregnancy: females slip their eggs into the male's pouch, and about 20 days later he gives birth to live young. Babies also hitch rides on floating debris to drift to new homes.
patagonian-seahorse.revealFact: The Patagonian seahorse lives along the coasts of south-eastern Brazil, Uruguay and Argentina. It is the seahorse most often caught in southern Brazil, mostly as bycatch of shrimp fisheries, and is also traded as curios, amulets and traditional medicine.

hints.habitat: Clinging to seaweed, seagrass, sponges or man-made structures in shallow coastal water
hints.size: Up to about 9.2 cm long
hints.diet: Small crustaceans, mainly amphipods and decapods

sunshine-pleco.funFact: This armoured suckermouth catfish is an aquarium celebrity with several stage names: 'sunshine pleco', 'goldie pleco', or simply its catalogue code, L-014.
sunshine-pleco.revealFact: The sunshine pleco lives in the Xingu River basin in Pará, Brazil, mainly around the Volta Grande do Xingu, with records reaching into the lower Iriri. It is listed as Vulnerable.

hints.habitat: Rocky rapids of a big river, hugging the bottom
hints.size: Up to about 29 cm long

piracanjuba.funFact: An endangered freshwater fish that can grow to nearly 80 cm, it roams both near the riverbed and up in midwater.
piracanjuba.revealFact: The piracanjuba lives in the large rivers of the Paraná–Paraguay–Uruguay (La Plata) basin, shared by Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay, and is listed as Endangered.

hints.habitat: Big freshwater rivers, between the bottom and midwater
hints.size: Up to about 80 cm long

marble-trout.funFact: Its skin looks like polished marble, and the pattern's intensity shifts with its surroundings. Its head is so big, up to a quarter of its body, that one local nickname simply means 'head'.
marble-trout.revealFact: Marble trout survive in only a handful of rivers draining to the Adriatic, in Italy, Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro, and are probably gone from Albania. Hybridisation with stocked foreign trout is one of their biggest threats.

hints.habitat: Cold, clean mountain streams and rivers over sand and gravel, rarely warmer than 15 °C in summer
hints.size: Up to about 120 cm (1.2 m) long, not counting the tail
hints.depth: Spawns in swift water about 0.6–0.8 m deep
hints.diet: Invertebrates when young; mainly smaller fish as adults

myaka.funFact: The only member of its genus, this little cichlid lives in open, deep water but heads for the shallows to breed in the rainy season, where crowds of males each guard a patch about 50 cm wide.
myaka.revealFact: The myaka lives only in Barombi Mbo, a small volcanic crater lake in western Cameroon, alongside three other endemic cichlid genera. Pollution and sedimentation from human activity threaten it, and gas released from the lake bottom is a potential risk too.

hints.habitat: Open, deeper water of a small crater lake
hints.size: Up to about 6.7 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Phytoplankton and small insects

natron-tilapia.funFact: This hardy cichlid thrives in extra-salty water at a toasty 30–32 °C. Males dig nest pits in the shallows, and mothers carry the young in their mouths.
natron-tilapia.revealFact: The soda tilapia lives only in the hot, hypersaline Lake Natron in Tanzania, its drainage, and the Shombole Swamps in Kenya. That tiny range is why it is classed as Endangered.

hints.habitat: Hot springs and lagoons around a very salty, warm lake
hints.size: Up to about 11.6 cm long
hints.diet: Mainly algae, plus copepods and fly larvae

burchells-redfin.funFact: Like all its close relatives, this redfin is tetraploid, carrying four sets of chromosomes instead of two. Youngsters gather in big shoals, while adults stick to small groups.
burchells-redfin.revealFact: Burchell's redfin survives in just two known populations in South Africa's Western Cape, in the Moeras and Tradouw rivers, which are cut off from each other when water runs low in summer. Introduced smallmouth bass, river changes and pollution have left it critically endangered.

hints.habitat: Pools and deeper, slightly peaty stretches of small rivers
hints.size: Up to about 13.5 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Detritus and small bottom-living organisms

fiery-redfin.funFact: In the breeding season males light up with bright red fins and defend their own patch of stream. Youngsters keep to the edges, while adults prefer calmer pools.
fiery-redfin.revealFact: The fiery redfin lives only in a handful of tributaries of the Olifants River system on the western side of the Cederberg Mountains, South Africa, where invasive bass, trout, carp and catfish threaten it.

hints.habitat: Clear, rocky streams with cobble riffles and pools
hints.size: Up to about 7.1 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Detritus and small bottom-living insects

red-stumpnose.funFact: Its scientific name means 'hump-head', after the bulging forehead that big adult males grow. It also answers to the nickname 'Miss Lucy', and its favourite prey is brittle stars.
red-stumpnose.revealFact: The red stumpnose is found only off the southern coast of South Africa, roughly from False Bay to East London. Adults live on offshore reefs while juveniles shoal over shallow rocky reefs, and the species is classed as Endangered.

hints.habitat: Rocky reefs in coastal seas; juveniles in the shallows, adults further offshore
hints.size: Up to about 75 cm long
hints.diet: Mainly brittle stars, plus crustaceans, molluscs, worms and small fish

somali-cavefish.funFact: This pale, scaleless, blind fish ignores the sun entirely: it was the first animal found whose body clock doesn't reset to daylight, running on cycles up to 47 hours long.
somali-cavefish.revealFact: Found only in underground waters of Somalia, reached through wells and caves around Bud Bud, it is thought to have been evolving in caves for some two million years. Somalia is home to two other cavefish species as well.

hints.habitat: Dark underground waters reached through wells and caves
hints.size: Up to about 6.2 cm long

lake-ifni-trout.funFact: Its back is marbled and its belly fins are tipped in black and white. A peek at its stomach contents turned up tiny crustaceans, land-dwelling arthropods and a dense mat of algae.
lake-ifni-trout.revealFact: The Ifni trout lives only in Lake Ifni, a high mountain lake smaller than one square kilometre in Toubkal National Park, in Morocco's High Atlas.

hints.habitat: A single small, high-altitude lake
hints.size: Up to about 18 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Tiny Cyclops crustaceans, land arthropods, filamentous algae and diatoms

deckerts-tilapia.funFact: Mum and dad pair up, dig a shallow nest pit beside a stone or branch, and guard their brood together. Cheeky youngsters have been seen nibbling the fins of other fish!
deckerts-tilapia.revealFact: Deckert's tilapia lives only in Lake Ejagham, a small lake in western Cameroon that turned out to hold six more endemic cichlids, described in 2010 and 2011. A recently introduced catfish is probably a serious threat to all of them.

hints.habitat: A small, fairly shallow freshwater lake
hints.size: Up to about 10 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.depth: Breeds in water shallower than 2 m
hints.diet: Zooplankton, copepods and a few insect larvae

bermin-tilapia.funFact: These cichlids lay their eggs on sunken wood, sometimes in neighbourhoods of about 10 pairs spaced just 30 cm apart, and pairs have even been seen guarding youngsters together.
bermin-tilapia.revealFact: This critically endangered cichlid lives only in Lake Bermin, a tiny crater lake in western Cameroon, where pollution and sedimentation from human activities threaten it.

hints.habitat: A tiny freshwater crater lake
hints.size: Up to about 8.2 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Mainly phytoplankton, plus plants and sponges

mafia-notho.funFact: This killifish is most common in temporary pools, spawning on the bottom, where its eggs take one to three months to develop. It honours the aquarist Edith Korthaus, who collected the first specimens.
mafia-notho.revealFact: Nothobranchius korthausae is found only on Mafia Island, Tanzania, in pools, swamps, ditches and small streams amid savanna-like vegetation and gallery forest.

hints.habitat: Temporary pools, ditches and small streams in savanna-like country
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm long

west-african-seahorse.funFact: Remarkably, this seahorse was first caught on video only in 2012, and scientists still know almost nothing about its life cycle. Dad does the egg-carrying, in a brood pouch under his tail.
west-african-seahorse.revealFact: The West African seahorse lives in coastal waters from Senegal to Angola, and has recently turned up in the Canary Islands, where it has hybridised with a local seahorse. Around 600,000 a year are exported for traditional medicine, mostly to China.

hints.habitat: Near the sea floor in shallow coastal waters
hints.size: Up to about 19 cm tall

kieneri-damba.funFact: This fairly slender cichlid might actually be more than one species hiding under a single name. It honours the fisheries scientist André Kiener.
kieneri-damba.revealFact: The kotsovato lives in rivers and lakes across several river basins of north-western Madagascar, and is threatened by habitat loss and competition from introduced species.

hints.habitat: Rivers and lakes, near the bottom
hints.size: Up to about 16 cm long, not counting the tail

saroy.funFact: This cichlid grows up to 25 cm and is at home in slightly salty brackish water as well as fresh.
saroy.revealFact: The saroy lives in streams of far north-western Madagascar and on the island of Nosy Be. The island population seems stable, but mainland populations are threatened by habitat loss.

hints.habitat: Freshwater streams near the bottom; also tolerates brackish water
hints.size: Up to about 25 cm long

trondo-mainty.funFact: A critically endangered cichlid of up to 24 cm, it shares its home waters with another cichlid that has probably already gone extinct.
trondo-mainty.revealFact: The trondo mainty is found only in the Onilahy River basin of south-western Madagascar, where habitat loss, fishing and introduced species threaten what remains of its small range.

hints.habitat: Near the bottom in a single river basin
hints.size: Up to about 24 cm long, not counting the tail

marojejy-bedotia.funFact: Only described by scientists in 2000, this little open-water fish takes its name from the national park beside which its first specimens were collected.
marojejy-bedotia.revealFact: Bedotia marojejy is known from the Manantenina River on the edge of Marojejy National Park in north-eastern Madagascar, and is threatened by habitat loss.

hints.habitat: Open water of forest streams
hints.size: Up to about 4.8 cm long, not counting the tail

powder-blue-panchax.funFact: This killifish is not one of the seasonal kinds, and aquarists find it hard to keep; it prefers a tank furnished with rocks, plants and driftwood.
powder-blue-panchax.revealFact: The powder-blue panchax is found only on the island of Nosy Be and in the Sambirano River basin and nearby streams on the adjacent mainland of north-western Madagascar.

hints.habitat: Quiet stretches of brooks and small rivers
hints.size: Up to about 9.5 cm long

pike-asp.funFact: This fish-eating river predator is the only species in its genus, and it was a common fish until the 1980s before its numbers crashed.
pike-asp.revealFact: The pike asp lives in rivers of the Aral Sea basin, such as the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, in Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan. After a rapid decline it is endangered there and has vanished from neighbouring Kazakhstan.

hints.habitat: Main channels of big rivers; rarely in lakes
hints.size: Up to about 50 cm long
hints.diet: Other fish

sharpray.funFact: It's the only species in its genus, yet it still manages to come in two recognised subspecies.
sharpray.revealFact: The sharpray lives in rivers of the Aral Sea basin, including the Syr Darya, Amu Darya and Zeravshan, in a region shared by Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

hints.habitat: Near the bottom of freshwater rivers
hints.size: Up to about 21 cm long

abant-trout.funFact: This vulnerable trout grows to about 30 cm, and its entire species lives in just one small lake.
abant-trout.revealFact: The Abant trout is found only in Lake Abant, a small mountain lake in Bolu Province, north-western Turkey.

hints.habitat: A single small mountain lake
hints.size: Up to about 30 cm long, not counting the tail

shabout.funFact: This giant carp can reach 2 m and 100 kg, yet it is mostly vegetarian, munching algae, water plants, fruits and even grain. A single female can lay over 235,000 eggs.
shabout.revealFact: The shabout lives in the Tigris–Euphrates river system of Turkey, Syria, Iraq and western Iran, plus Iranian rivers draining to the Persian Gulf. Dams, water extraction, drought, pollution and overfishing have driven its decline.

hints.habitat: Rivers from upstream tributaries to their mouths; also marshes and reservoirs
hints.size: Up to about 150 cm (1.5 m) long; reportedly up to 2 m
hints.diet: Mostly plants (algae, water plants, fruits and grain), plus some invertebrates and small fish

pnar-cavefish.funFact: This is the biggest known cave-dwelling fish, and oddly its eyes shrink out of sight as it grows: juveniles have obvious eyes, while the largest adults barely seem to have any.
pnar-cavefish.revealFact: Neolissochilus pnar lives in the Krem Um Ladaw and Krem Chympe caves in the Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, north-eastern India. First seen in the 1990s, it was only collected and photographed for study in 2019, and is named after the local Pnar people.

hints.habitat: Pools in a seasonally flooded cave with a rocky floor
hints.size: The largest known subterranean fish
hints.diet: Possibly plant debris washed in by seasonal floods

blotched-filament-barb.funFact: Each of these barbs stakes out a territory several square metres wide, yet fish of the same size still hang out together in loose schools.
blotched-filament-barb.revealFact: The blotched filament barb lives only in the Kalu River basin of south-western Sri Lanka, where tailings from upstream mines push it toward extinction. It has recently been bred at the Dehiwala Zoological Gardens.

hints.habitat: Midwater in fast-flowing river stretches over pebbles, never silt
hints.size: Up to about 10 cm long

sinarapan.funFact: Barely 2.5 cm long, this goby is see-through, with just a few dark spots and a pair of black eyes. It's also the only member of its genus.
sinarapan.revealFact: The sinarapan lives only in Lake Buhi, a few nearby lakes and the Bicol River in Camarines Sur and Albay on Luzon, Philippines. Overfishing and introduced Nile tilapia pushed it near extinction, so thousands were moved to safer lakes, where they were breeding by 2001.

hints.habitat: Freshwater lakes, from the shoreline down to about 12 m
hints.size: Up to about 2.5 cm long

lanao-barb.funFact: This endangered member of the carp family grows to about 13 cm and roams between the bottom and midwater of lakes and rivers.
lanao-barb.revealFact: Barbodes tumba is found only in Lake Lanao and its connected waters on Mindanao, Philippines.

hints.habitat: Lakes and rivers, between the bottom and midwater
hints.size: Up to about 13 cm long, not counting the tail

reticulated-hillstream-loach.funFact: Instead of hopping rock to rock like its cousins, this loach launches off a high rock and glides on the current before landing. It also flutters its fins over sand to uncover food.
reticulated-hillstream-loach.revealFact: The reticulated hillstream loach lives in fast hill streams of central Vietnam, in the provinces of Thua Thien-Hue, Quang Nam, Quang Ngai and Binh Dinh.

hints.habitat: Shallow, fast, oxygen-rich streams with riffles, pools and waterfalls
hints.size: Up to about 5.7 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Algae and tiny organisms grazed off surfaces, plus the odd insect larva

licorice-gourami.funFact: Less than 3 cm long, this gourami is the type species for its entire genus. It honours a military health officer who sent fish specimens to the scientist who described it in 1859.
licorice-gourami.revealFact: The licorice gourami is found only on Bangka Island in Indonesia, in slow blackwater streams of peat swamp forests.

hints.habitat: Slow, dark-watered creeks among plants in peat swamp forest
hints.size: Up to about 3 cm long, not counting the tail

sichuan-taimen.funFact: A glacial relic of the salmon family, it spawns in water of just 4–9 °C, burying its heavy yellow eggs in nests dug into the soft riverbed.
sichuan-taimen.revealFact: The Sichuan taimen survives only in cold headwaters of the upper Yangtze basin in China, in tributaries such as the Min and Dadu in Sichuan and Qinghai and the Han River system in Shaanxi. It is critically endangered and has lost much of its genetic diversity.

hints.habitat: Fast, cold, oxygen-rich mountain brooks with sand and gravel beds, 700–3,300 m above sea level
hints.size: Up to about 64 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Aquatic insects, worms and smaller fish; zooplankton when young

kanglang-fish.funFact: This open-water minnow is losing a battle for food against an introduced rival with a delightful name: the noodlefish.
kanglang-fish.revealFact: The Kanglang fish lives only in Fuxian Lake in Yunnan, southern China, where competition with the introduced noodlefish Neosalanx taihuensis may be pushing it toward extinction.

hints.habitat: Open water of a single freshwater lake
hints.size: Up to about 15.6 cm long, not counting the tail

taiwan-angelshark.funFact: This flat, ray-like shark buries itself in the sediment to ambush prey, with its eyes perched on top of its head. Oddly, the lower lobe of its tail is bigger than the upper one.
taiwan-angelshark.revealFact: The Taiwan angelshark is found only on the continental shelf off Taiwan, between about 20° and 24° N. It is a frequent bycatch of bottom trawling, and its population is suspected to have fallen by 50–80%.

hints.habitat: Buried in sediment on the outer continental shelf
hints.size: Up to about 55 cm long (possibly larger)

biwa-giant-catfish.funFact: The top predator of its home waters, this giant catfish hunts fish and frogs, yet it's a homebody that mostly stays close to its spawning grounds.
biwa-giant-catfish.revealFact: The Lake Biwa giant catfish lives only in Lake Biwa in Japan, where it is the largest predatory fish, and it is the biggest of Japan's silurid catfishes. It even appears in Japanese mythology, where a giant catfish named Namazu causes earthquakes.

hints.habitat: Near the bottom of a big freshwater lake
hints.size: Up to about 118 cm (1.2 m) long
hints.diet: Fish and frogs

honmoroko.funFact: This endangered gudgeon goes by the bouncy common name 'honmoroko' and spends its time between the lake bottom and midwater.
honmoroko.revealFact: The honmoroko, or Biwa moroko gudgeon, lives only in Lake Biwa in Shiga Prefecture, Japan, and is listed as Endangered.

hints.habitat: Between the bottom and midwater of a single big freshwater lake

itasenpara.funFact: Also known as the deepbody bitterling, this little fish tops out at a maximum length of just 8 cm.
itasenpara.revealFact: The Itasenpara bitterling is endemic to central and southern Japan, living in floodplain waters of the Nōbi Plain (Kiso–Nagara rivers), the Toyama Plain and the Yodo River.

hints.habitat: Fresh waters on low-lying river floodplains
hints.size: Up to about 8 cm long

weedy-seadragon.funFact: Disguised with leafy flaps that mimic seaweed, it drifts rather than swims and can't grip with its tail like a seahorse. Dad carries around 120 eggs stuck under his tail for about a month.
weedy-seadragon.revealFact: The weedy seadragon lives only along Australia's temperate southern coast, from Western Australia to New South Wales and around Tasmania. It is the marine emblem of the state of Victoria.

hints.habitat: Rocky reefs, kelp and seaweed beds and seagrass meadows
hints.size: Up to about 46 cm long
hints.diet: Tiny crustaceans and other zooplankton, sucked up through a tube-like snout

northland-mudfish.funFact: When its swampy home dries out over summer, this mudfish simply waits it out in damp spots under tree roots and logs. Its species name means 'marsh dwelling'.
northland-mudfish.revealFact: The Northland mudfish is found only in a few swampy peat wetlands west of the Bay of Islands in Northland, New Zealand, and in 2026 it won New Zealand's Fish of the Year competition.

hints.habitat: Peaty swamps and wetlands that dry out over summer
hints.size: Up to about 11.8 cm long

dalhousie-goby.funFact: This tiny goby can tolerate water as hot as 43 °C, though it usually stays below 36 °C. Adults are also known to eat their own young.
dalhousie-goby.revealFact: The Dalhousie goby lives only in Dalhousie Springs in Witjira National Park, South Australia, in about 28 of roughly 148 isolated springs fed by the Great Artesian Basin. It is the smallest of five fish species found nowhere else but these springs.

hints.habitat: Shallow, warm, reedy edges of spring-fed pools and swamps
hints.size: Up to about 4.5 cm long, not counting the tail
hints.diet: Filamentous algae, small molluscs and crustaceans, and sometimes its own young

leopard-epaulette-shark.funFact: Covered in dense leopard-like spots with a big black eyespot behind its head, this little shark went unrecognised until 2010, when a photographer noticed it was different and it was named after him.
leopard-epaulette-shark.revealFact: The leopard epaulette shark is known only from shallow reefs of eastern Papua New Guinea, mostly in Milne Bay Province. It was long confused with the Indonesian speckled carpetshark until it was described as a separate species in 2010.

hints.habitat: Coral reefs, rocky outcrops, tide pools and seagrass beds
hints.size: Up to about 70 cm long

cenderawasih-epaulette-shark.funFact: This small shark often 'walks' across the seabed on its fins. Its species name honours a photographer who made a winning bid at a charity auction to help conserve it.
cenderawasih-epaulette-shark.revealFact: Hemiscyllium galei is known only from shallow reefs in Cenderawasih Bay, West Papua, Indonesia, and was scientifically described only in 2008.

hints.habitat: Fringing and patch reefs, resting under rocks or corals by day
hints.size: Up to about 57 cm long

northern-river-shark.funFact: Known only by a placeholder label, 'Glyphis species C', until it got a proper name in 2008, this tiny-eyed shark lives in murky, silty water with big tides. Its young roam into fresh water, but adults stay in the sea.
northern-river-shark.revealFact: The northern river shark is found in scattered tidal rivers and coastal waters of northern Australia (the Kimberley and the Northern Territory) and southern Papua New Guinea. Very rare, it is threatened by commercial and recreational fishing.

hints.habitat: Murky tidal rivers, estuaries and coastal bays with muddy bottoms
hints.size: Up to about 145 cm (1.45 m) long
hints.diet: Probably fish

oopu-nakea.funFact: Its diet is about 84% stringy algae with a side of non-biting midges. Males build the nest, and both parents stand guard over the eggs.
oopu-nakea.revealFact: ʻOʻopu nākea lives only in streams of the main Hawaiian Islands. Once lumped in with a related goby, it was recognised as a distinct species thanks to differences in body form and genetics.

hints.habitat: Freshwater streams, swimming upstream against strong currents
hints.diet: Mostly filamentous algae, plus non-biting midges

robertsons-wrasse.funFact: This little wrasse seeks out rough water, favouring reef slopes pounded by strong waves. It is named after a scientist honoured for his studies of reef fishes.
robertsons-wrasse.revealFact: Robertson's wrasse is known only from the waters around Clipperton Island in the eastern Pacific, and is named after Dr D. Ross Robertson of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute.

hints.habitat: The outer reef slope, where surge is strong
hints.size: Up to about 7.8 cm long, not counting the tail

galapagos-barnacle-blenny.funFact: This blenny moves into empty barnacle shells, poking out only its head and darting out to grab drifting bits of food. Dad guards the eggs stuck to the walls of the shell home.
galapagos-barnacle-blenny.revealFact: The Galápagos barnacle blenny is found only on reefs of the Galápagos Islands, and is named after Miguel Castro, a naturalist at the Charles Darwin Foundation on Santa Cruz Island.

hints.habitat: Empty barnacle shells on reefs
hints.size: Up to about 6 cm long
hints.diet: Bits of floating food

cocos-barnacle-blenny.funFact: Barely 3 cm long, this blenny lays its eggs on the walls of its shelter, where dad stays on babysitting duty.
cocos-barnacle-blenny.revealFact: The Cocos barnacle blenny lives only in the waters around Cocos Island (Isla del Coco), Costa Rica.

hints.habitat: On the bottom of rocky reefs; common in the shallows
hints.size: Up to about 3.2 cm long, not counting the tail

malpelo-barnacle-blenny.funFact: A tiny house-hunter, this blenny moves into empty barnacles and abandoned worm or mollusc tubes, and snaps up passing zooplankton.
malpelo-barnacle-blenny.revealFact: The Malpelo barnacle blenny is found only on reefs around Malpelo Island, Colombia, in the eastern Pacific.

hints.habitat: Empty barnacles and worm or mollusc tubes on rocky reefs
hints.size: Up to about 5 cm long
hints.diet: Zooplankton

black-striped-salema.funFact: Sporting seven black stripes along its silvery sides, this grunt forms dense daytime schools along rock walls. Its species name honours the describing scientist's second wife, Jessie.
black-striped-salema.revealFact: The black-striped salema lives only in the waters around the Galápagos Islands, where it was first described in 1890 from Isla Santa María.

hints.habitat: Rock walls and rocky slopes, in big daytime schools
hints.size: Up to about 30 cm long
hints.diet: Plankton and small fishes

red-striped-wrasse.funFact: This little wrasse picks an unusual neighbourhood: sandy seabeds sprinkled with fine rubble, where it lives down to at least 30 m.
red-striped-wrasse.revealFact: The red-striped wrasse is found only around Cocos Island (Isla del Coco), Costa Rica; close relatives fill the same sandy-rubble niche on the mainland and at Malpelo Island.

hints.habitat: Sand scattered with small rubble of volcanic rock chips or chalky algae, near reefs
hints.size: Up to about 6.3 cm long, not counting the tail

st-helena-wrasse.funFact: So little is known about this wrasse that its habitat entry on FishBase is still flagged as 'needs verification'.
st-helena-wrasse.revealFact: The St Helena wrasse is found only in the waters around St Helena in the South Atlantic, in shallow coastal water near rocks and rocky reefs.

hints.habitat: Shallow coastal water near rocks and rocky reefs
hints.size: Up to about 18.7 cm long, not counting the tail

madeiran-ray.funFact: Its belly starts out smooth but turns prickly with age, and it lays eggs whose shells sport horn-like projections.
madeiran-ray.revealFact: The Madeiran ray seems to be found only on the shelf and upper slope around Madeira, Portugal, although similar skates reported from the Azores may turn out to be the same species.

hints.habitat: Hard and soft seabeds of the continental shelf and upper slope
hints.size: Up to about 85 cm long
hints.diet: All kinds of bottom-dwelling animals

south-georgia-icefish.funFact: A 'crocodile icefish' with a forward-curving spine on its snout, three lateral lines and big fan-shaped pelvic fins, it dines mostly on krill.
south-georgia-icefish.revealFact: The South Georgia icefish lives in shelf waters around South Georgia, the Scotia Sea and the northern Antarctic Peninsula. It was listed as Endangered in 2024, though a 2026 study argued that the assessment relied on outdated data and that the species is not clearly declining.

hints.habitat: Near the seabed in continental-shelf waters
hints.size: Up to about 60 cm long
hints.diet: Mainly krill and other fish
